title: NC State, UNC to meet in inaugural 'Tobacco Road Classic' in Greensboro in December
description: One of college basketball's oldest rivalries is getting a new touch.
fullText:
One of college basketball's oldest rivalries is getting a new touch.

The University of North Carolina and NC State University announced their men's basketball programs will meet in the inaugural 'Tobacco Road Classic', a non-conference, neutral-site game to be held at First Horizon Coliseum in Greensboro.

"For the fans, it's a fun rivalry," said NC State head coach Justin Gainey. "I look forward to (as we lead up to that game) talking to our guys about the history of the tradition, and all the great coaches and players that have played in that rivalry."

The 2025-25 season was the first time since 1919 that long-time rivals did not play twice in the regular season. Because of league expansion, the ACC reduced its league schedule from 20 games to 18, which in turn forced the ACC to assign each school one "primary partner" to play home and away.

For UNC, that was Duke, and for NC State, that was Wake Forest. But the creation of this new event guarantees two of the state's most proud programs will meet twice in the regular season this year and next.

"The landscape is changing, but we have to make sure as caretakers of this game that we're finding ways to give back to the fans and give them what they want," said UNC head coach Michael Malone.

"UNC-NC State is one of the greatest rivalries in college basketball, and we're thrilled to bring it to Greensboro," said Scott Johnson, General Manager of First Horizon Coliseum.

"The Tobacco Road Classic gives fans the opportunity to experience this historic matchup in a neutral-site setting, and we're grateful to the universities, athletic directors, and coaches for making this game possible."

Tickets go on sale on Thursday, September 10th at Ticketmaster.com and the First Horizon Coliseum Ticket Office.

The December 15th game will mark the first time UNC and NC State will play in Greensboro in the regular season since they met in the Big 4 Tournament on November 30th, 1979.

title: Greatest college football personalities? Finebaum reacts to being ranked ahead of Tebow, Saban
description: Tell us where they got it wrong.
fullText:
As we prepare to embark on yet another college football season, The Sporting News took a look at the 25 greatest college football personalities of all time.

Any college football fan will recognize the names. Some are coaches, while others are players. Broadcasters and media types populated the list, too.

"As someone who gets a little tired of college football lists, I must confess I found this one fairly fascinating," ESPN's Paul Finebaum told this reporter about being ranked No. 6 on the list right behind former Oklahoma linebacker Brian Bosworth and right in front of former Florida coach Steve Spurrier. "Being ranked ahead of Tim Tebow and Nick Saban in anything is a career bucket list."

Agree or disagree with the order of the list, but clearly most of these names belong here.

"The 'The Paul Finebaum Show' soared in popularity during the SEC's stranglehold of college football during the BCS and four-team College Football Playoff era," The Sporting News reads. "Finebaum's understated delivery, strong opinions and self-deprecating sense of humor rile up callers who stir the pot for arguments that often cross over into Big Ten country. It makes for some of the most entertaining material in the social-media era, and Finebaum continues to contribute to being the leading provocateur in the sport."

Broadcasters dominate the top of the list.

Former ESPN and "College GameDay" host Lee Corso comes in at No. 1 followed by the late "Pope of College Football" Beano Cook.

Former Mississippi State coach, the "Pirate" himself, the late Mike Leach ranks No. 4.

Rounding out the top 10: (7) Steve Spurrier, former Florida coach, (8) Lou Holtz, former coach and broadcaster, (9) Nick Saban, former coach and now broadcaster and (10) Tim Tebow, former player and now broadcaster.

Saban is one of two former Alabama coaches to make the list with Paul "Bear" Bryant listed at No. 12.

The Big Ten gets some love with former Ohio State coach Woody Hayes at No. 22.

Yes, we mentioned mascots. Oregon's duck Puddles (No. 24) and Georgia's Uga (No. 13) are on the list.

Check out the full list and tell us in the comment section what they got wrong and who was left out.

title: DOJ opens probe into prestigious college over alleged discrimination favoring minority students
description: The Department of Justice is probing whether the College of William & Mary's scholarships and programs favor racial minorities in violation of Title VI.
fullText:
The Department of Justice launched an investigation on Monday into the College of William & Mary to determine whether certain scholarships and student benefits at the Virginia-based public research institution include unlawful race-based criteria, adding to the Trump administration's targeting of educational institutions across the country.

The DOJ's Civil Rights Division announced it was opening a compliance review for the college's potential violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color or national origin in programs or activities receiving federal financial assistance.

"Awarding scholarships or offering coveted opportunities to students based on the color of their skin is illegal and offends the guarantees of our color-blind Constitution," Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon said in a statement.

"We will find out if scholarships or other student benefits at William & Mary favor applicants of certain races. The Department will not turn a blind eye to race-based preferences, however they are packaged or portrayed by universities," she continued.

Doj Opens Probe Into Harvard's Financial Aid For Alleged Discrimination Against American Students

The "W&M Scholars" program for first-year undergraduate students includes a scholarship that covers at least the full cost of in-state tuition and fees.

While the scholarship is not limited to any particular race, the DOJ said in a notice letter to the institution that applicants with an "interest in diverse people and perspectives" receive "top consideration." William & Mary's website lists that consideration alongside academic ability and potential and first-generation or limited-income status.

The W&M School of Education's need-based Martha L. Muguira Fellowship for graduate students gives a "preference" to Hispanic or Latino women, who have financial need, according to the DOJ. The W&M School of Education's doctoral-level Holmes Scholars program was described by the DOJ as giving "future education leaders of color" mentorship, access to job fairs and position announcements, as well as national-level professional development benefits, including policy and advocacy training and opportunities to present their research. William & Mary's current website describes Holmes Scholars as students "from traditionally under-represented backgrounds."

The DOJ said the W&M Law School offers the Lemon Legal Scholars Program. The DOJ said W&M Law offers up to five full scholarships covering tuition and fees that appear to be exclusively for HBCU graduates. William & Mary's current website, however, says the law school "will award at least five full scholarships" to HBCU graduates admitted to its J.D. program.

Recipients of this scholarship also receive networking opportunities, one-on-one academic advising regarding course load and bar exam preparation, as well as access to special events with W&M Law School faculty, senior administrators and alumni.

The law school also advertises the "Reaching Back Scholarship," which is a need-based scholarship that has a "preference" for HBCU graduates or those "who contribute to the diversity" of W&M Law School, the DOJ said.

Some programs at the institution were established to deal with the legacy of slavery and racial discrimination at William & Mary.

The DOJ urged William & Mary to hand over certain documents and information by September 8 as part of the compliance review. The department said ⁠it wants ​to secure compliance by "informal voluntary means" ​but may take formal action such as proceedings that could result in the termination of federal financial assistance if it deems such a move necessary.

Doj Sues Ucla Over Alleged 'Judenrein' Conditions During Anti-israel Encampment

Responding to the federal probe, William & Mary said in a statement that it is "committed to nondiscriminatory learning environments across our campus and complying with all state and federal laws."

The DOJ's Civil Rights Division said it had not reached any conclusions about the subject matter of the investigation.

This is just the latest effort by the Trump administration to target educational institutions across the nation for issues such as race-based admissions and scholarships, diversity, equity and inclusion programs and alleged antisemitism on campus.

title: Andy Beshear calls socialism a 'failed experiment' as poll finds Dems view it more favorably than capitalism
description: Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear called socialism a "failed experiment," but said he supported abolishing the electoral college and overturning Citizens United.
fullText:
Democratic Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear called socialism a "failed experiment" on Sunday, addressing a new poll that found socialism was viewed more favorably than capitalism by Democrats.

CBS News' Ed O'Keefe asked Beshear about a CBS poll that found 58% of Democrats have a positive view of socialism, compared to just 32% who have a positive view of capitalism.

"What I make of it is that people are struggling. They're struggling because the cost of groceries is too high. The cost of gas is too high. It's too hard to see a doctor, and when you do, the cost of that is too high as well. They're not asking for a lot," Beshear said on "Face the Nation."

He continued, "And right now, they're seeing a system that doesn't work for them. Now, I believe socialism is a failed experiment, but I do believe that we need to get results for the American people, and I think when you look at Democratic governors, you see those results."

Beshear cited some of his work in Kentucky and said Americans just want to see results.

Capitalism Is About Incentives. Stopping The Stupidity Of Socialism Is A Big Incentive

Economist Michael Szanto told Fox News Digital that Beshear was right to call socialism a failed experiment.

"Despite talk that Americans are starting to lean towards socialism, they are really voting with their smartphones and fingers. More Americans are engaged with the stock market than ever before. Gen Z is really the Robin hood generation as once etrade had captured the speculative energy of Gen X and older millennials," he said.

Szanto said Republicans and Democrats needed to be able to address the affordability crisis.

He added, "Many Americans are sympathetic to elements of socialism because they recognize that key institutions like Medicare, public libraries and public schools are technically socialist. They also recognize the existence of mainstream democratic socialist parties in Europe like Germany's SPD."

"On the other hand, the Democratic Socialists of America have a radical agenda that is diametrically opposed to our capitalist and democratic system and completely inconsistent with mainstream American values. Democrats will not be able to consistently win elections despite President Trump's high level of unpopularity if they are allowed themselves to get tied to the radical DSA," the statement continued.

Author and psychotherapist Jonathan Alpert told Fox News Digital that he also felt Beshear was right to be frustrated.

"I think Beshear is right about the frustration, but the rise in support for socialism shouldn't be mistaken for a sudden ideological conversion," Alpert said.

"That frustration creates fertile ground for socialism because socialism offers a very seductive message: The system is rigged, your struggles aren't your responsibility, and government can make things fair. When people feel stuck or powerless, that can be an appealing promise," Alpert said.

"The danger for Democrats is confusing economic frustration with a mandate for socialism. There's a huge difference between voters saying, 'Capitalism isn't working for me' and saying, 'I want socialism.' Democrats would be smart to address the first without embracing the second," he continued.

Kamala Harris Is The 'Fairly Obvious' 2028 Presidential Frontrunner, Democratic Insiders Say

O'Keefe asked the Kentucky governor about a big and bold idea he was promoting, noting another portion of the CBS poll that found Democrats want their leaders pushing to make big changes.

"Well, I'll give you two because people want you to fix the darn economy, and they want you to fix the darn government. On the economy, it is time for an aspirational investment in housing that can bring down the cost of especially first-time home ownership," he said.

Beshear said fixing the government meant outlawing partisan redistricting, "enshrine part of the Voting Rights Act right there in the Constitution" and instituting term limits for Congress and the Supreme Court.

"It should also overturn Citizens United, and I think call for direct elections of the president and the vice president. That could actually make things work. A big idea that would, yes, change government, but in a way enshrined in the Constitution where people would know it's going to get better," he added.

"I didn't realize you support abolishing the Electoral College. If you're saying direct election of the president and vice president," O'Keefe said.

Beshear responded, "Yeah, I've said it a number of times, and it's because in Kentucky we will never see a candidate for president or vice president unless they're from here. Why? Because people just expect that it'll go one way or the other. It's the idea that someone would get elected not just knowing about seven states, but having to earn votes all over the United States. I certainly think it's time."

Former Vice President Kamala Harris also recently expressed wanting to change the Electoral College. Both Harris and Beshear are considered potential presidential contenders for the Democratic Party in 2028.

However, Beshear said he was still deciding on whether he was planning to run during the interview.

The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Kentucky Republican National Committee and Kentucky Democratic National Committee did not immediately return Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

title: Meet Daniel Hughes, the most interesting man in college football
description: A fascinating look into a fascinating Seminole newcomer.
fullText:
Levels of interest aren't exactly at their peak surrounding Florida State football entering the 2026 season.

And yet, the Seminoles have a new player in New Mexico transfer punter Daniel Hughes who has a compelling case for being the most interesting man in college football.

At 16, he dropped out of Year 10 (sophomore year of high school) in Australia, began a carpenter apprenticeship, was fully qualified by 19 and launched his own business.

So how did he end up as a college punter and internet content creator?

"I was not happy with what I was doing," Hughes said. "I was making a really good living, retired my mom. I was really comfortable. But money doesn't buy happiness, and I always want to be a professional athlete."

And so, he went back to secondary school (what high school is called in Australia), got his Year 12 pass (high school diploma) and got involved with ProKick Australia, even though he was much older than many of the other people in the program.

"About 25, 26, you sort of finish up your career sort of like towards 30," Hughes recalled. "I'd seen ProKick and I saw athletes that were over here that were half the athlete that I am. I was like, 'I can kick a ball, man.' So, I reached out to them."

After a few other stops, he's now 28 years old and using his final year of collegiate eligibility at Florida State.

When he was punting at his first American school, City College of San Francisco in the junior college ranks, he launched his social media account.

It grew mildly then and last season at New Mexico, but has really blossomed this offseason since joining the Seminoles. He has over 50 thousand followers on Instagram and over 25 thousand on TikTok.

There's football and punting galore on his accounts, but also day-in-the-life content, vlogs and various other forms of content.

Hughes says it's grown enough by now that he pretty much always gets recognized in public when he's out in Tallahassee, but that it's been an extremely positive experience.

"The community is great. I can't go to Publix or Whole Foods now without getting recognized. It's always really positive encounters, it's just 'How's the season going? How are you looking? I love your content, it brings such a positive light on the program and even some people's lives as well,'" Hughes said. "I get messages from people saying, 'Hey man, I was going through a really dark time and your content has like brought me into now going to the gym and just doing some really good things now.' So, in terms of the community stuff, it's always positive. But yeah, I can't really leave the house now without getting recognized."

Hughes' distinctive look certainly doesn't hurt his online presence. He's 6-foot-5, 219 pounds (down about 30 from when he arrived at FSU, he says) with much of his body covered in tattoos. While he's sporting long black hair in his FSU headshot, he's since dyed his hair a shade he calls blond but could certainly be construed as Targaryen grey.

Although he admits the content will be a bit slower for the next few months with football season upon us, he also believes his natural approach to being on camera has helped his viewership blossom.

"My content is very genuine and authentic," Hughes said. "There's no like, 'Oh my god, look at me. I'm going to fake this.' It's 'this is what I'm going through in life right now. How can I portray that to the Florida State fans and my community as well?'"

Now, to simply discuss his content is to overlook the fact that Hughes has established himself as a very strong punter in his own right.

Hughes' lone season at New Mexico under first-year head coach Jason Eck was a massive success, with the team jumping up five wins in 2024 to nine (tied for the most in program history since 1982) last fall.

He ranked 29th in FBS in average yards per punt (45.4) last season for the Lobos. In the much more important net yards per punt stat (average punt distance minus average punt return allowed), Hughes ranked seventh among players with 30-plus punts at 43.0 yards.

In his interview this past Thursday, he was quick to not take too much credit for that.

"(Net punting) is a unit statistic. It's not a Daniel Hughes or a punter statistic. So it was a unit statistic," Hughes said. "I just played my role in that stat."

New special teams coordinator Adam Scheier, who coached against Hughes last season when he was on UNLV's staff, felt more comfortable lauding him with praise and hyping up that net punting stat when asked about him that same day.

"I watched his stuff, and he's a very talented punter," Scheier said of Hughes. "Those guys joke all the time, right? I've got three things that are really important to me in life: my wife, my kids and net punt. So it will carry over. We will make an emphasis of attacking that unit as an opportunity to flip the field, because our job at the end of the day is to play great defense, and the way you do that is you move the ball as far down the field as you possibly can, give your defense as long a field to defend as possible, and I think it'll carry over."

Hughes, named to the Ray Guy Award watch list on Friday, did admit he's very confident in his ability to make all types of punts which could be required of him this season. He sees some similarities between the culture at New Mexico and what he's been around in Tallahassee, and is hopeful a similar leap up in success will be the product of that.

Until the games begin, Hughes is just prepping for that moment and relishing in where his truly unique journey has taken him.

"Every day, I wake up with a smile on my face. I get in my car at five in the morning, I'm so excited to come here. I was talking with Duce Robinson last week, and he was like, 'I'm so excited for you to see the warchant for the first time.' I think the first time when we come out of that tunnel, that's when I'd be like, I'm at Florida State."

title: Grantsville rallies from 12-point deficit, scores 30 unanswered to stun San Juan 30-20
description: For the first quarter and a half against Grantsville Friday, it looked like San Juan was going to remind everyone why it was one of the most dangerous offensive teams in Utah.  Then Grantsville’s defense took over.  The Cowboys erased a 12-0 deficit by scoring 30 unanswered points, forcing seven San Juan turnovers along the way, and held on for a 30-20 victory at Snow College.
fullText:
For the first quarter and a half against Grantsville Friday, it looked like San Juan was going to remind everyone why it was one of the most dangerous offensive teams in Utah.

Then Grantsville's defense took over.

The Cowboys erased a 12-0 deficit by scoring 30 unanswered points, forcing seven San Juan turnovers along the way, and held on for a 30-20 victory at Snow College.

It was a game that seemed to change every few minutes. San Juan came out firing as quarterback Beau Yeomans opened the scoring with a 1-yard touchdown run, and later in the first quarter he found Brigg Palmer wide open for a 47-yard touchdown.

Just like that, San Juan had a 12-0 lead.

And then the Broncos stopped scoring, although it took a while for the Cowboys offense to get going as they threw two interceptions deep in San Juan territory.

But Grantsville's defense kept giving the offense another chance.

"We left a lot of points on the board," Grantsville coach David Millward said. "We had interceptions in the end zone. I think we had four red-zone possessions without points."

Eventually, though, the Cowboys broke through when Carter Bell scored on a 9-yard run early in the second quarter, cutting San Juan's lead to 12-7.

Then late in the first half, Mack Hammond intercepted Yeomans and gave Grantsville the ball at its own 42. Crew Allred immediately ripped off a 34-yard run, and then with 2.4 seconds left before halftime, Allred rolled to his left and found Ty Holm for a 24-yard touchdown.

Suddenly, the team that had trailed 12-0 was leading 13-12.

The Cowboys opened the second half by forcing another San Juan turnover when Palmer fumbled at the San Juan 30.

Grantsville turned that opportunity into another touchdown, with Bell punching it in from the goal line. A successful two-point conversion pushed the lead to 21-12.

Bell added another touchdown later in the quarter, this one on a 7-yard toss play, and Cache Hammond's 37-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter made it 30-12.

That was 30 straight points for Grantsville.

San Juan finally showed some life again late in the fourth when Yeomans found Palmer for a 39-yard touchdown with 5:25 remaining and Randall Black ran in the two-point conversion to make it 30-20.

The Broncos got one more chance when they forced Grantsville to punt, but after driving deep into Cowboys territory, Yeomans threw another interception to Graeson Warren.

That was Warren's second interception of the night and effectively ended San Juan's final serious threat.

For Millward, the biggest thing wasn't that his team played a perfect game. It absolutely didn't. It was that the Cowboys kept fighting anyway.

"I'm just so proud of our kids," Millward said. "They just battled and battled, and we made a lot of mistakes, but they just kept believing."

Grantsville's defense did more than just create turnovers. It swarmed San Juan throughout the night.

"They just swarm and swarm," Millward said. "That's what we like to say, that we just play hard-nosed football in Grantsville, and I feel like tonight, that's what we did."

And that's probably the best way to describe the game. San Juan looked like the better team early, then Grantsville made play after play.

For a Grantsville team that spent much of the first half leaving points on the field, its defense made sure it would get enough chances to eventually make them count.

And when the Cowboys finally did, they didn't stop.

fullText:
CHAMPAIGN, Ill. (WCIA) - No one on Illinois football's 2026 team has score more touchdowns in an Illini uniform than Kaden Feagin.

The rising senior has found the end zone 15 times through his first three years of college ball, 12 on the ground and three receiving. Aidan Laughery has the second most with eight.

Now, the Arthur, Ill. native makes the move from running back to tight end for the 2026 season. Instead of boasting an ego for his several touchdowns and more than 1,500 all-purpose yards, Feagin asked for criticism from his peers when joining the tight end room.

"All the tight ends were working after a lift and I'm like 'Hey, Christian, if you see me doing anything wrong you can tell me. It's not going to make me mad or anything. Be hard on me, be critical,'" Feagin said.

Christian Abney is a fellow-senior in the tight end room, with the difference being he has been playing that position throughout his college career. Abney played two seasons at Ball State before joining the Illini prior to the 2025 season.

Feagin says new Illini tight ends coach Jared Elliott, who coached Abney at Ball State in 2024 before working with New Mexico in 2025, has helped cultivate a tight-knit, eager to learn position group.

"I feel like all the guys, we could go up to each other and be like 'Hey, you did this wrong, you did that wrong.' But it's just all out of love," Feagin said.

Abney says Feagin's open invitation for helpful feedback opened the door for him to be honest and insightful as the ALAH grad joined the TE room.

"It really just shows his humility," Abney said. "Someone who has played that much good football over the years, and has done so well at one position, and wants to come to another one. He is going to be great at it because of his humility, and because of his ability to improve at things and realize what he needs to improve on. Him saying something like that is just a testament to how he goes about his business, and the type of person he is."

Feagin also says the tight end room has made it a priority to connect older and younger players together. Davin Stoffel is another veteran in the room who has played a fair amount of football, coming to the Illini before the 2025 season after two years at South Dakota State.

Notably, all three of the seniors listed about would seemingly be eligible, if interested, for a fifth year of eligibility under the NCAA's new rule allowing athletes to compete in five seasons across five years.

title: AD Alford: ‘Excitement Around Seminoles Football is High’
description: Florida State athletic director Michael Alford was interviewed on the ACC Huddle: Florida State Road Trip. He offered some insights into how Florida State is competing with its peers in the arena of college athletics.
fullText:
For thelast seven years, Florida State athletic director Michael Alford has crisscrossedthe southeastern portion of the United States championing his university toboosters, parents and potential student athletes.

His mission: raise funds andrecruit talent to Florida State.

On the ACCHuddle-Florida State Road Trip show, Alford was interviewed, and he offeredsome insights into the "business" end of college football.

"When I arrivedsix, seven years ago, Florida State was not up to par to what our peers were,and we had to invest in the resources," said Alford. "Offering a holistic view,we have a top 25 public education we can offer, now we got these facilities.And, when you come and train mind, body and soul, then you have to invest in thetalent acquisition. We are doing that at a high level and giving them the bestof both worlds in coming to Florida State. It really represents what FloridaState is about, the class of this university, the community and our program."

So far,this year has been the most successful year of fundraising for Florida Stateboosters, bringing in a record-setting $106 million. Alford and his departmentare committed to providing all that is necessary to help his teams be competitive,and ultimately win.

"You haveto invest and give them the resources," said Alford. "In the last severalyears, we've done over $550 million in renovations. We are giving them theresources, now they got to go produce."

Unfortunately,that production has not materialized on the gridiron for the Seminoles. 17losses in their last 24 games is not a good return on investment, by anymeasure. But as the new season approaches, Alford said. "Excitement around thisteam is high."

Astraining camp draws to a close and the week zero game with New Mexico State is uponus, fans and the media could see coach Mike Norvell lead a different FloridaState team out of the tunnel at Doak Campbell Stadium.

Men with adesire to be better versions of themselves, to play together as a band ofbrothers, forged in blood, sweat and tears. They endured the blistering summerheat to transform themselves into warriors in search of gridiron glory, notonly for themselves, but for a grateful fan base.

Players flirtedwith the transfer portal, but changed their minds and returned because they believedin their development within the Seminoles program. Coaches stayed, trained theirplayers hard over the summer leading up to fall camp. title: BC Football Countdown to Kickoff 2026: Duke Preview
description: Boston College will face a new-look Blue Devils team this season.
fullText:
Halloween falls on a Saturday this year and that means Boston College will be in action.

The Eagles will face off with ACC foe Duke in what is its second straight road game and part of a stretch of three out of four.

Head Coaches: Bill O'Brien, Boston College; Manny Diaz, Duke

When: Saturday, October 31 at TBD

Where: Wallace Wade Stadium in Durham, North Carolina

The history between these two teams dates back to 1927 when they first played in Chestnut Hill, Mass. After meetings in three consecutive seasons, they did not play until 2006. There has been a total of nine matchups between Boston College and Duke with the Eagles holding a 5-4 advantage. Duke has won three of the last four.

What a year it was for the Blue Devils. Duke began 1-2 after a loss to Tulane before ripping off three straight wins. The Blue Devils had another bad loss to UConn midseason but won the final three games, including the ACC Championship against Virginia. The Blue Devils would go on to win the Sun Bowl, 42-39, over Arizona State.

Darian Mensah was going to return to Duke this fall but the transfer portal era got in the way. Miami came calling with what has to be a nice offer to play quarterback and he headed to South Beach.

This leaves the Blue Devils without their leader who threw for close to 4,000 yards and 34 touchdowns last year. In comes Walker Eget from San Jose State. He has been thrown to turning the ball over but has a big-time arm. Dan Mahan has not played yet but was a highly-valued recruit last year as well.

Not only did Mensah head south, but Duke lost its top pass catcher as Cooper Barkate will join his quarterback in Miami. He led Duke with 1,106 yards and seven touchdowns last season. Qua'Sean Brown (Virginia Tech) and Sahmir Hagans (graduated) are also gone. This leaves Duke without its top three pass catchers.

This means tight end Jeremiah Halsey will have to take on more responsibility while transfers Jared Richardson and Javen Nicholas will be thrown into the mix right away.

It also looks like Nate Sheppard will be relied upon more heavily after an All-ACC season where he totaled 1,132 rushing yards and 11 touchdowns. He will be running behind a new offensive like with Braden Miller (Cal) and Nick Del Grande (Coastal Carolina) coming to play tackle, joining center Matt Craycraft and guard Jordan Larsen.

Manny Diaz knows how to coach up a defense and we saw this last season.

This defense last year was strong up front and took the ball away often but struggled on third down and in the passing game.

The Blue Devils forced 24 turnovers last season and multiple in seven games. The middle of the defense will be just as good with Luke Mergott and Kendall Johnson returning. The duo combined for 127 tackles last season. Throw a healthy Nick Morris in the mix and the linebackers are elite.

The defense needed four new starters up front after coming away with 11 or more tackles for loss in six games.

The secondary lost Chandler Rivers and Caleb Weaver as well. The defense allowed 276.8 passing yards per game and 45% or worse on third downs eight times.

This being a late October matchup means we will likely know the direction of Boston College's season by this point. The major question is — can the Eagles pull off an upset over the reigning ACC champs?

Duke's offense will look completely different but by this point of the season, it will not be a new-look group anymore. It will be interesting to see if the Eagles can take advantage of the new faces though and get in the backfield. This is another game where the Eagles will be getting points and at this time, it is hard to imagine an upset. But anything is possible!

Will the Eagles be able to earn a statement victory heading into November?

fullText:
Alabama continues to have a competitive quarterback battle ahead of the college football season, but the Crimson Tide appear to be leaning in a particular direction. Austin Mack is battling former touted recruit Keelon Russell to be Alabama's QB1.

The early signs point to Russell having the edge over Mack in the quarterback competition. On3's Pete Nakos reported that it was Russell who was most impressive during Alabama's scrimmage on Thursday, August 13.

"Sources who watched Thursday's scrimmage said both quarterbacks had strong moments, but it was the former five-star recruit Russell who was making plays," Nakos wrote in an August 13, story titled, "Inside Alabama's first scrimmage with Austin Mack, Keelon Russell battling for QB job."

"That has been the buzz for most of camp, with Mack stringing together consistent day after consistent day while Russell has moments where he dazzles," Nakos added.

"With Alabama still working through some preseason challenges with its offensive line, Russell's ability to stretch plays with his legs has been evident, sources told On3. One source told On3 that Russell looked like a 'stud' at Thursday's scrimmage."

Let's dive into the latest college football news and rumors.

Both Mack and Russell are believed to have lucrative NIL deals. Mack's projected NIL value is $2.2 million, per the NIL Standard.

Russell has a confirmed NIL deal of $2 million with Alabama, per On3. Whatever direction Alabama goes, the team is likely going to have an expensive backup quarterback waiting on the sideline.

There is no potential timeline for when Alabama will announce their final decision at quarterback, per Nakos. Alabama takes on East Carolina on September 5.

"As the scrimmage went on, they both got better," DeBoer said of the quarterbacks, per Sports Illustrated. "Had their moments early where they could have executed better. They could use some help from some guys once in a while. They're not going to be perfect all the time.

Russell played in two games for Alabama in 2025 completing 11-of-15 passes for 143 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions.

title: Returning Rockford Boylan players are convinced they can bounce back this season
description: Boylan High School very rarely goes through head coaching changes, but the Titans are this year. Joel Beard is the guy now, a coach with a lot of college coaching experience in his background at the junior college level.
fullText:
ROCKFORD, Ill. (WTVO/WQRF) — Boylan High School very rarely goes through head coaching changes, but the Titans are this year. Joel Beard is the guy now, a coach with a lot of college coaching experience in his background at the junior college level.

There are two things that we do know about Beard already. He is fired up to be coaching the Titans, and he's known for overseeing explosive, high-scoring offenses in the past at the College of DuPage. That's the type of offense he ultimately wants to have at Boylan.

"We like to be explosive. Make some explosive plays and get everybody involved. We like to be multiple that way and keep defenses guessing."

"He's working us really hard," said Boylan senior linebacker/tight end Nick Polivka of his new head coach. "This is going to be my fourth year, and this is probably the hardest summer since I've been here. I'm really excited."

The coaching change from former coach John Cacciatore to Beard, and a 2-7 season last year for Boylan, led to several key players transferring to other NIC-10 schools. The Titans are ready to roll though with who they have, and they believe there's more than enough talent here to have a bounce-back season.

"We're going to rock with who we've got," said Polivka. "We've got, I think, the best guys. I'm very confident in our team with what we've got going."

Polivka is part of a linebacker unit that should be very strong. Eyzaiah Campos will be one of the other outside linebackers, and in the middle will be junior Keaton Hampl. He missed some time last year with an injury. Hampl is ready to roll. He has the size and aggressiveness to be a beast.

"He's going to anchor our defense," said Bear.

"It feels great to be out here 100 percent," said Hampl who missed most of last season with an injury."

The Titans also have an experienced safety in Henry Maier, and a couple linemen up front who will be impact players on defense, Erick Becerra and Edy Espinoza.

On offense, senior Michael Davenport takes over at quarterback. He has some good targets in Jake Fowler and athletic receiver Mikele Sims. Basketball has been Sims' sport, but now he is giving football a shot, and he looks like he could be one of those explosive playmakers that Beard wants.

When the Titans run the ball, Sam Bland and Campos will be doing most of the work. Espinoza, Becerra, Peyton Kirchner and Caleb Gork will provide the blocking up front.

title: SN 140: The top college football teams of each decade dating back to the 1800s
description: See how the bluebloods became the bluebooods.
fullText:
SN 140: The top college football teams of each decade dating back to the 1800s originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

College football has been evolving in hyperspeed the last five years and shows no signs of slowing down. And yet, the more things change ...

As part of Sporting News' year-long celebration of 140 years of publishing, we took a look back at a sport that loves its history and traditions perhaps more than any other in the U.S. Last week, SN named seven All-Decade All-America teams, starting in the 1960s. This week, we are going all the way back, to when we published our first newspaper, when touchdowns were four points and field goals were worth five. We are naming our top program of each decade -- with some being obvious and some being absolutely not obvious.

But it is interesting to note, teams that were at the top of the sport in the '40s, '50s, '60s, '70s and '80s will be contending for College Football Playoff spots in 2026. If you want to learn how the modern-day bluebloods of the sport became blueboods, read about their dominance from decades ago.

We hope you enjoy your trip back in time as we look ahead to 140 more years of publishing (and college football!).

SN 140 ALL-AMERICA TEAMS BY DECADE:2020s|2010s | 2000s | 1990s | 1980s | 1970s | 1960s

SN 140: Greatest college football teams of all time

National titles: 1874, 1876, 1877, 1880, 1881, 1882, 1883, 1884, 1886, 1887, 1888, 1891, 1892, 1894

Why they are here: By the time The Sporting News published its first newspaper in 1886, Yale had put together 10 unbeaten seasons and were retroactively awarded eight national championships by the National Championship Foundation. The following 15 seasons brought more glory, as Walter Camp became the team's first official coach in 1888 and proceeded to go 68-2 in his first five seasons. (Princeton and Harvard bested the Yaleies). Captains served as coach before then, and Camp was the captain for three of his playing seasons. He was also instrumental in several rule changes that slowly made the violent, brutal nature of the first iterations of the game slightly less violent and brutal.

Honorable mention: Princeton and Harvard gave Yale the most competition, and Penn emerged late in the 1890s, but had stopped playing Yale at that point. The only non-Ivy League school to claim a national championship in the 1800s was 1896 Lafayette, which went 11-0-1 with the tie coming against Princeton.

National titles: 1901, 1902, 1903, 1904

Why they are here: Fielding Yost took the reins of the Michigan program in 1901 and proceeded to steamroll everything in its path in his first five years. Michigan went 11-0 in his first year and beat Stanford 49-0 in the Rose Bowl, finishing the season with 550 points scored and 0 allowed. In '02, they allowed six points during another perfect season. A 6-6 tie against Minnesota was the only blemish in 1903 and 1904 produced another perfect season that included a 130-0 win over West Virginia. The Wolverines were 55-1-1 in Yost's first five seasons. They outscored Ohio State 285-18 for the decade, finishing 9-0-1 against their rivals.

Honorable mention: Yale notched 100 wins, with most coming against major competition as college football was more established in the Northeast. The Bulldogs were awarded the 1900, 1907 and 1909 national titles, plus had undefeated seasons in 1902, 1905 and 1906. Princeton, Penn and Harvard were also Northeast powers, while Michigan's competition in the Midwest came from Chicago under Amos Alonzo Stagg and Minnesota.

Why they are here: John Heisman (yes, the Trophy guy) had quite a run in Atlanta, going 24-0-2 from 1915-17 against what was considered a difficult schedule at the time. Included in that stretch was the Yellow Jackets' infamous 222-0 win over Cumberland. The 1917 national championship team gave up just 17 points in nine games and Tech had a winning record all 10 years of the decade.

Honorable mention: Minnesota remained a Western Conference power with a 52-13-4 record. Pitt was retroactively awarded three national titles in 1910, 1916 and 1918 (with a war-shortened 4-1 record), the latter two under coach Pop Warner. Pitt matched Georgia Tech by going undefeated from 1915-17. Vanderbilt and Auburn were consistently elite, and Harvard owned New England football at the time with a gaudy 65-7-5 record.

Why they are here: Knute Rockne took over in 1918, went undefeated in 1919 and rolled through the '20s suffering either no losses or one loss in eight of the 10 seasons. Legend has it he was an early adopter of the forward pass, and his Irish traveled coast-to-coast and created a national following. By 1928, ND went east to play Penn State, south to play Georgia Tech and west to play USC. That type of travel was unique to the Irish at the time.

Honorable mention: Cal picked up two national titles and had five undefeated seasons while winning at an .805 percentage for the decade. Vanderbilt (68-17-7) and Alabama (74-21-6) were early powers in the new Southern Conference. Cornell went 24-0 from 1921-23 under Gilmour Dobie, though the 1923 national title went to Champions of the West(ern Conference) – Michigan.

National titles: 1934, 1935, 1936

Minnesota won the first AP national championship in 1936 after a pair of undefeated seasons in 1934 and 1935 that were retroactively awarded national titles by the Helms Athletic Foundation and the NCF. Coach Bernie Bierman had a record of 93-35-6 from 1932-50.

Honorable mention: Notre Dame was 66-20-5 (.753) with just nine winning seasons in a decade where the program had to overcome the loss of coach Knute Rockne in a plane crash after his undefeated 1930 season. ND wasn't able to quite match the gold standard Rockne established but remained elite. USC won 72 games and was 30-2-1 with two Rose Bowl wins from 1931-33. Alabama was 79-11 but somehow did not win a national championship.

National titles: 1943, 1946, 1947, 1949

Why they are here: When World War II ended, Notre Dame fielded a juggernaut that did not lose a game for four years. Frank Leahy's squad went 36-0-2 in the first four seasons after the war, which added to a 1943 national title led by Heisman winner Angelo Bertelli. The Irish claimed two other Heismans in the decade as well and was the sport's dominant program.

Honorable mention: Army went a perfect 16-0 with back-to-back national titles in 1944-45 and went 9-0-1 in 1946 with a famous 0-0 tie against Notre Dame. Army won 67 games, two Heismans and was ranked in seven of the 10 seasons. Minnesota started the decade with a pair of undefeated, national championship seasons led by 1941 Heisman winner Bruce Smith.

National titles: 1950, 1955, 1956

Why they are here: The team that put together a mid-decade 47-game winning streak was a pretty clear winner. That streak remains unmatched at the FBS level. The Sooners won three consensus national titles, which was not an easy thing to do with four outlets declaring national champions (1954, 1957 and 1958 were all split). OU was ranked all 10 years and only twice lost more than one game. Bud Wilkinson's squad ruled the decade.

Honorable mention: Ohio State won one AP national title in 1954 and a UPI national title in 1957 after winning Rose Bowls under Woody Hayes. Bobby Dodd was 79-26-6 at Georgia Tech playing in the SEC, including 6-0 in bowl games. Ole Miss won 80 games and finished No. 2 in 1959, and Notre Dame ended OU's winning streak and had three Top 5 finishes.

National titles: 1961, 1964, 1965 (split)

Overall record: 90-16-4 (55-12-2 SEC)

Why they are here: Bear Bryant quickly restored power in Tuscaloosa after Jennings Whitworth went 4-24-2 from 1955-57. By the time the '60s rolled around, the Tide was ready to roll through the decade. The 1965 'split' title was only split because UPI voted before bowl games and gave Michigan State the title before the Spartans lost the Rose Bowl. In 1966, 11-0 Alabama finished behind Notre Dame and Michigan State, who went undefeated but tied each other. Bama finished in the top 5 five times in the '60s.

Honorable mention: Texas won consensus titles in 1963 and 1969 and piled up 86 wins. One ding to the resume was four seasons where the Longhorns finished unranked. USC matches Texas with two national titles and two unranked seasons, and adds Heismans from O.J. Simpson and Mike Garrett. Woody Hayes had Ohio State rolling as well with one national title and four top five finishes, but there were five seasons the Buckeyes finished unranked.

National titles: 1974 (split), 1975

Why they are here: Oklahoma owned the best winning percentage among major programs, it won two AP national championships, and would have had two UPI national championships if Barry Switzer's undefeated 1974 team wasn't on probation (UPI did not vote for teams on probation). The Sooners had an average final ranking of 4.7 in the AP poll and were ranked all 10 seasons, plus produced Heisman Trophy winner Billy Sims. OU went 7-3 vs. Nebraska, which averaged 9.8 wins per year.

Honorable mention: USC was right there, with 1 AP and 3 UPI national titles (including the above-mentioned '74). It was ranked all 10 years, won 93 games and owned a very good ND program. Alabama won 90 percent of its SEC games and 103 games overall, and was only hurt by a 6-5-1 record in 1970. Nebraska won two AP national titles and finished ranked all 10 years, and Notre Dame averaged 9.2 wins per season for the decade and also won two AP national titles. This decade was the toughest debate.

National titles: 1983, 1987, 1989

Why they are here: Miami's three national titles came under three different head coaches, with Howard Schnellenberger shocking Nebraska in 1983, Jimmy Johnson steamrolling to an undefeated season in 1987 and Dennis Erickson capping the decade with a third championship. The Hurricanes also had two No. 2 finishes in the AP poll and won their final 32 games at the Orange Bowl (bowl games included) in the 1980s.

Honorable mention: Nebraska won 103 games and finished in the AP Top 11 every year. A 4-6 record in bowl games and no national championships are the only negatives on the resume. The 1983 team lost 31-30 to Miami in the Orange Bowl after winning their first 12 games by an average of 36 points. Oklahoma had four Top 6 seasons, won four Big 8 titles over Nebraska, won 91 games and the '85 national championship. Penn State won 89 games and two national titles, but had four unranked seasons.

Overall record: 109-13 (62-2 ACC)

Why they are here: The most amazing FSU stat for the '90s? The Seminoles finished in the AP Top 4 all 10 seasons. Florida State went an incredible 109-13 and captured national titles in 1993 and 1999. It was a tight battle with Nebraska for Program of the Decade, but the Noles finished ahead of the Huskers in the AP poll seven times. FSU also won both head-to-head matchups, beating them in the Fiesta Bowl after the 1992 season and the Orange Bowl in the 1993 season that gave Bobby Bowden his first national title. The 1999 squad was the first wire-to-wire No. 1 team of the AP era.

Honorable mention: In Tom Osborne's final five seasons from 1993-97, Nebraska lost just three games. The Huskers also closed the decade with a 12-1 season in 1999. The Huskers finished in the top 6 six times and the 1995 team is considered one of the sport's best of all time. FSU's two head-to-head wins give it the slightest of edges over Nebraska here.

National titles: 2004, 2005 (split)

Overall record: 102-26 (64-20 Pac-10)

Why they are here: This one was tight. USC opened the decade with a couple of duds, but Pete Carroll got things rolling to the point that his 2005 team was being discussed as the best of all time … before it lost in the final seconds to Texas and Vince Young in one of the great games of all time. Carson Palmer, Reggie Bush and Matt Leinart all won Heismans, and USC was 37-2 from 2003-05. The final eight years of the decade, USC went 13-0 vs. the Big Ten/SEC and 8-0 against Notre Dame.

Honorable mention: Florida and LSU both had claims as both won more than one national title. The Gators had two championships in three years, with Tim Tebow seeing spot duty in 2006 and then becoming larger than life in 2008. Florida won an even 100 games for the decade. LSU went 99-31, shared the 2003 title with USC under Nick Saban and won the 2007 title under Les Miles. Georgia won 98 games and had three Top 10 finishes.

National titles: 2011, 2012, 2015, 2017

Overall record: 124-15 (69-11 in the SEC)

Why they are here: Alabama was ranked No. 1 in the AP poll at some point during the season every season of the decade, and was ranked no lower than No. 3 in the AP preseason poll each season. It was Nick Saban's world, and everyone was living in it. They won two titles with AJ McCarron, who threw 179 career NFL passes. They won another with Jake Coker, who threw none. The fourth title came with Jalen Hurts, but he was benched in the CFP championship. Eighty-three players were drafted in the decade, including 28 in the first round. When Alabama lost in the 2010s, it was breaking news.

Honorable mention: Clemson only lost two regular season games in the final five seasons of the decade, collecting two national championships along the way. It beat Alabama twice in the national championship game, the second by a stunning 44-16 margin. The Tigers were eye-to-eye with the Saban Machine in the second half of the decade.

Overall record: 73-9 (44-5 in the SEC)

Why they are here: The Bulldogs are the only team to win multiple national titles this decade and they finished in the top seven of the final AP poll every year. Georgia made the last five SEC Championship Games, winning three and they became the first back-to-back national title winners since Alabama in 2011-12. Georgia's 2022 title team averaged 46.6 points per game and gave up 18.8 in its five games against ranked opponents, including a 65-7 demolition of TCU in the national title game.

Honorable mentions: Ohio State reached two national title games, winning one and is 66-11. Alabama also reached two national title games, winning one, and had four top-five AP finishes in six years.

title: Louisville adds North Carolina transfer G Seth Trimble
description: Seth Trimble, who spent the last four seasons playing key roles at North Carolina, is transferring to Louisville for his final year of college hoops. Trimble, who entered the transfer portal in the spring, became an option for Louisville to add after a Colorado district court ruling last month that gave Class of 2022 high […]
fullText:
Seth Trimble, who spent the last four seasons playing key roles at North Carolina, is transferring to Louisville for his final year of college hoops.

Trimble, who entered the transfer portal in the spring, became an option for Louisville to add after a Colorado district court ruling last month that gave Class of 2022 high schoolers an extra season of college eligibility.

As a "senior" in 2025-26, Trimble averaged 14.0 points and 3.0 assists per game for the Tar Heels. He scored a career-high 30 points in a win over Louisville. Perhaps most notably, Trimble hit the game-winning shot at the buzzer un UNC's upset of arch-rival Duke.

After going undrafted in June, Trimble averaged 10.8 ppg for the Washington Wizards in the NBA's Summer League. He did not, however, sign an official contract with the Wizards, a move which left the door open for him to return to college.

Known for his defensive prowess and ability to attack the rim than his outside shooting (28.6 percent from three last year), Trimble is an interesting add for a Louisville team that seemed to be more or less set in the backcourt. I suppose when you have the opportunity to add an experienced, All-ACC caliber performer, you take it regardless of your current situation.

One thing that Trimble absolutely adds that U of L may have been lacking is a knack for making the biggest play at the biggest moment. It's not just the Duke shot, either. Look at how many of the plays in this reel are game-saving, game-winning type plays.

Seth Trimble is a Louisville Cardinal! pic.twitter.com/FHrrBRufml

To quote Jeff Brohm, "all we can do right now is the use the current rules that are out there to the best of our advantage."

These are strange times, bit if you're standing still when you have the opportunity to move forward, you're basically moving backwards.

Now the big question will become whether or not PK and company are done with preseason acquisitions.

title: This Missouri school named the best community college in the nation
description: See why WalletHub ranked this Missouri community college as the best in the nation.
fullText:
Community colleges can offer students a quality education and access to career opportunities post-graduation, at a fraction of the cost of many four-year institutions.

For instance, during the 2025-26 school year, tuition for a full-time undergraduate program at a public four-year university was nearly three times higher on average than tuition at a public two-year in-district community college, according to College Board.

For those considering the community college route, you'll find one of the best in Missouri.

WalletHub, the personal finance company released a study examining the best and worst community colleges in the country for 2026.

WalletHub ranked State Technical College of Missouri No. 1 in its community colleges ranking.

In its analysis, WalletHub compared more than 610 community colleges across 18 key indicators, including cost of in-state tuition and graduation rate. Those metrics were then grouped into three categories — Cost & Financing, Education Outcomes and Career Outcomes — to determine each state's overall score.

State Tech ranked among the top five nationally for both education outcomes and career outcomes, which isn't too surprising given the school bills itself as "The Employers' Choice." Its score in cost & financing, meanwhile, was more middle-of-the-road.

State Tech earned a total score of 73.99 out of 100.

title: Kalshi’s 30-year-old CEO says most business advice is ‘trash’—he doesn’t read management books or listen to podcasts: ‘I’m gonna make it up as I go’
description: Kalshi cofounder Tarek Mansour slams founders for being over-reliant on ‘mostly trash’ business advice—he founded his now-$22 billion prediction market as a college grad.
fullText:
Prediction market Kalshi has exploded in recent years, reaching a $22 billion valuation. For the company's 30-year-old CEO, Tarek Mansour, getting there hasn't meant following the wisdom of business school professors or management gurus—it's been ignoring advice altogether.

"The worst advice that most people get is that you should go and seek out a bunch of advice. There's really no recipe to any of this stuff," Mansour told The New York Times in a recent interview. "People are over-reliant on advice, and people love giving advice because it makes them feel smart and powerful. It's usually mostly trash."

Mansour's skepticism of conventional founder wisdom is backed by his own track record: He and cofounder Luana Lopes Lara have built Kalshi into a platform with four million active users and became self-made billionaires, with estimated net worths of about $2.6 billion each.

And when it comes to his own business approach, Mansour said he's largely learned by doing—opting to even ignore management books or podcasts.

"I have a lot of, I'm gonna make it up as I go," he said on a Sequoia Capitol podcast last month.

"Both of us, we're probably very sort of entrepreneurially illiterate," Mansour said, referring to himself and his cofounder, Lopes Lara. "We haven't read all the books, we haven't watched all the podcasts."

Mansour and Lopes Lara met as classmates at MIT, and with companies like Goldman Sachs, Palantir, Citadel, and Bridgewater Associates on their collective resumes, they were likely headed down lucrative careers in tech and finance.

Instead, less than a year after graduating, they set out to build Kalshi in 2018—initially envisioning the company as a financial exchange where users could buy and sell contracts tied to the outcomes of real-world events. The early years, however, were anything but easy. Kalshi faced regulatory hurdles as it sought approval for its novel business model, and Mansour admitted there were countless times when he wanted to give up.

"Every day you wake up and you're like, 'What am I doing?'" he said.

title: University of Michigan changes grade policy for some freshmen
description: The pilot program will apply only to some first-year students at one college.
fullText:
Thousands of freshman students at the University of Michigan will not see letter grades on their report cards next fall.

The school recently announced it is starting a "grade covering" pilot program in 2027 for all incoming first-year students in the College of Literature, Science, and the Arts, for their first semester, where students will only receive pass (P) or no credit (NC) grades instead of A through F letter grades.

Instructors and professors would still assign letter grades for students to know, but students' final GPAs and final transcripts for the first semester would not reflect them.

The school's college, which enrolls about 3,500 first-year students across over 80 majors, said the grade-covering program would benefit students' mental health.

"We believe that covering grades will help students start strong and curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals," the school explained, adding that the change will help "foster an environment where college students can acclimate to the demands of a University of Michigan education and pursue new academic challenges."

The policy change will not apply to other first-year students in the university's other 18 colleges, such as the business or engineering schools.

CDC launches new national campaign to tackle mental health, substance use among teens

Derek Peterson, a professor of history and African Studies and former chair of the university's Faculty Senate, told ABC News he welcomes the new grade policy change for LSA freshmen, some of whom he will be teaching in the fall.

"Mental health is a real problem for undergraduates here in Michigan, as it is across higher education," Peterson said. "Whatever we can do in terms of policy to enable our students to thrive in a difficult and challenging world that bears on their mental health profoundly, I think that's very much the right thing for us to do."

Peterson pointed out that many undergraduate freshmen are navigating new and transitional periods in their young lives, including balancing jobs, moving away from home and societal and familial pressures and the grade policy will enable them to experiment with new classes without the major consequences behind a class failure.

"First-year students are in a particularly precarious position," Peterson said. "The right response is to be charitable, to find ways to work with what our students do know how to do, to give them the space they need to figure it out, so that even if they aren't as well prepared, they can get up to speed in their first year and succeed thereafter."

Meta ordered to pay $567M by New Mexico court over child mental health harm

The University of Michigan declined to comment further on the new policy to ABC News.

The school is not the first higher education institution to implement a grade covering policy. Other schools such as the California Institute of Technology, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College and Wellesley College already have grade covering policies in place for first-year students.

title: Former UNC offensive coordinator unhappy about his time in Chapel Hill
description: UNC had one of college football's worst offenses under Freddie Kitchens during 2025. Now at Clemson, Kitchens reflected on his time in Chapel Hill.
fullText:
The UNC football program pressed a hard reset after its 2024 season, firing Mack Brown and hiring 8-time Super Bowl champion Bill Belichick as head coach.

One of Belichick's first staff additions was former Cleveland Browns head coach Freddie Kitchens, whom he retained from Mack Brown's staff to be his first offensive coordinator at North Carolina. The Tar Heels then went on to sport one of college football's worst offenses in 2025, averaging a measly 288.8 yards and 19.3 points per game.

Now a "volunteer offensive assistant" on Dabo Swinney's staff at Clemson, Kitchens threw shade when asked about his brief time at UNC, according to a recent article by The State's Chapel Fowler.

"When everything went down at Chapel Hill, I knew I wanted to get back with people that I trusted and I respected," Kitchens said. "I don't think I was chasing anything (at North Carolina). "It's just that sometimes...you don't do as much investigating as you should. I don't care to say anything about it. It's in the rearview mirror and I'm glad that aspect of my life's moved on. It's been great to be here at Clemson."

North Carolina only scored over 30 points once in 2025, a 41-6 blowout of Richmond, which plays at the FCS level. The Tar Heels scored a combined 19 points over their next three games, including just 10 during a 28-point loss in Death Valley.

For the reasons listed above, UNC fans don't exactly hold Kitchens in the highest regard either. He largely struggled with NFL offenses, then hit a new low with North Carolina's 2025 offense.

The Tar Heels now have former Arkansas head coach Bobby Petrino as their 2026 offensive coordinator. He's a significant upgrade from the disgruntled Kitchens, who looks for a fresh start in the Upstate.

title: The 20 best college towns where life revolves around their universities, ranked
description: College towns offer student experiences that set them apart from big cities. Life in Ann Arbor revolves around the University of Michigan's culture.
fullText:
College towns offer unique student experiences that set them apart from big cities.

For many, large research universities anchor the local economy and culture.

Ann Arbor tops the list of best college towns, driven by the University of Michigan's rich culture.

For many students, college is a time filled with rigorous classes, internship applications, and energy-drink-filled all-nighters.

College towns often offer a unique experience that helps these students manage flourishing social lives and hobbies alongside their academic careers.

Business Insider looked at some of the cities and towns across America where students can thrive, and compiled a list that best matches the loose definition of a college town.

To do so, we used data from the Census Bureau's latest population estimates and from WalletHub's 2025 ranking of the best college towns. We then filtered out major cities, focusing instead on places where colleges and universities anchor the local economy and lifestyle.

Not all college towns are built the same, however, and while some are extensions of nearby metropolises, others are smaller communities tucked away from other urban areas.

School: Brigham Young University

Nestled between mountains in the Utah Valley, the city of Provo is home to the private Brigham Young University, which has a student population of over 35,000 students.

The town has a lively economy, a young population, and its local culture is closely tied to religion and sports. Locals often enjoy the city's unique access to hiking trails and stunning natural landscapes.

School: University of Tennessee — Knoxville

Home to the University of Tennessee — Knoxville and its over 40,000 students, the city of Knoxville is a vibrant and energetic community.

The city is considered a gateway to the Great Smoky Mountains — as it's located less than an hour away from unique Appalachian landscapes — and a hub for country music, which soundtracks the city's scene.

During gamedays, over 100,000 fans pack into the school's Neyland Stadium in their best orange-and-white attire.

Located between Austin and Houston, College Station, Texas, is one of the state's best college towns. The city's culture, economy, and lifestyle are shaped by Texas A&M University.

The land-grant, SEC university has one of the largest student populations at its College Station campus, with over 72,000 students.

School culture unites the city, with Aggie pride inescapable on gamedays as fans congregate at the school's Kyle Field, which seats over 100,000.

The city is also home to the George H.W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum.

17. Chapel Hill, North Carolina

School: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

The school's roughly 34,000 students shape local culture and economy. Along with Durham — home to Duke University — and Raleigh — home to North Carolina State University — Chapel Hill is part of North Carolina's Research Triangle, a region where tech and education are among the most popular fields of employment.

Thanks to the college's prevalence and the region's entry-level job opportunities, the town has a highly educated, uniquely young population.

School: Michigan State University

Neighboring the state capital of Lansing, the city of East Lansing combines college culture with government employment.

The city is home to roughly 52,000 students at Michigan State University, which dominates local culture and sports. The school's sprawling campus sits directly across the city's downtown. Restaurants, cafés, shops, and bars cluster around the university.

15. San Luis Obispo, California

School: California Polytechnic State University.

Halfway between San Francisco and Los Angeles, the town of San Luis Obispo combines the energy of a college town with the laid-back lifestyle of California's Central Coast.

The over 20,000 students at Cal Poly have easy access to the region's beaches, mountain trails, and wine country, while the city's compact downtown is filled with restaurants, shops, and nightlife.

School: University of Connecticut

Population: 15,979 (per the 2020 census)

In the small community of Storrs, which is surrounded by the forests and farmland of northeastern Connecticut, the University of Connecticut is the center of life.

Downtown Storrs, located next to campus, has more than 70 businesses, as well as nature preserves and hiking trails. The university's size gives the otherwise rural community a steady stream of restaurants, events, arts programming, and student activity, especially during UConn basketball game days.

School: Harvard University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology

Few American cities have an academic identity as strong as Cambridge. With Harvard and MIT anchoring higher education in the city, the opportunities available attract thousands of students, researchers, and academics from around the world.

Harvard Square mixes restaurants, shops, museums, and entertainment around Harvard's historic campus, while Kendall Square, beside MIT, has become a hub for jobs in technology, biotechnology, and startups.

The city's location across the Charles River from Boston also gives students easy access to the metropolis's jobs, nightlife, and culture via public transit.

The University of Georgia's historic campus sits directly across from downtown Athens, making the city one of the most recognizable college towns in the South.

Athens has a prominent music scene that produced famous bands like R.E.M. and the B-52s, and live music remains a major part of the city's identity. Its walkable downtown is packed with local restaurants, bars, coffee shops, boutiques, and music venues.

On fall weekends, Georgia Bulldogs football takes over the city as tens of thousands of fans pack Sanford Stadium.

School: Washington State University

Tucked among the rolling hills of southeastern Washington, Pullman is a small town where Washington State University defines local culture and identity.

The compact downtown is within walking distance of campus and has many locally owned restaurants, coffee shops, and retailers.

The city's remote location contributes to a close-knit student and faculty community. School traditions and Cougar sports play a major role in local identity, which is also influenced by the natural landscape that surrounds the city.

School: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

The University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign spans the neighboring cities of Champaign and Urbana and is home to one of the Midwest's largest college communities, with over 59,000 students.

The university's research focus also extends to the local economy, with its Research Park and business incubator supporting technology companies and startups, and drawing students to remain in the area for internships and jobs long after graduation.

Located on Wyoming's high plains between mountain ranges, Laramie combines a historic Western downtown with the culture of the state's flagship university.

The over 10,000 students at the University of Wyoming have easy access to hiking, mountain biking, climbing, skiing, and other outdoor activities in the surrounding mountains and forests.

The city's downtown adds restaurants, coffee shops, breweries, and local businesses within a relatively compact area near campus, and the college culture also spans museums, performing arts, and Wyoming Cowboys athletics.

Purdue University's large student body of nearly 58,000 makes West Lafayette one of the most university-driven communities in the Midwest.

The school's reputation in engineering, science, and technology contributes to a local economy centered on research and innovation, while Big Ten athletics give the city's culture a strong sense of school spirit.

School: University of California, Berkeley

UC Berkeley's academic reputation and history of student activism have helped shape the city's culture for generations.

Just south of campus, Telegraph Avenue remains one of the city's most distinct student districts, with streets lined with independent stores, restaurants, and record shops.

Students can also head into the Berkeley Hills to explore beautiful trails and parks or easily reach San Francisco and other Bay Area communities through public transportation.

School: University of Wisconsin—Madison

Built between two lakes, Madison gives students a unique mix of a major state capital, a large Big Ten university, and easy access to the outdoors.

The city's State Street serves as the main connector between campus and the Wisconsin State Capitol, with cafés, restaurants, bars, galleries, and shops lining the corridor. On warm days, students gather along Lake Mendota at the university's Memorial Union Terrace.

College sports, cycling, lake activities, farmers markets, and a strong local food scene keep the city lively year-round.

Schools: Florida State University, Florida A&M University

Florida's capital city has one of the largest and most varied student communities on this list, anchored by multiple public colleges.

Florida State University and Florida A&M University each bring distinct traditions to the city, and along with the local Tallahassee State College, the city has a student population of over 65,000.

FSU's Seminoles generate major football weekends around Doak Campbell Stadium, while FAMU, one of the country's most prominent historically Black universities, has its own deep academic, cultural, and athletic traditions.

The city is also the center of the Florida state government and offers plenty of opportunities for students interested in politics, public policy, law, and government.

Located in the center of North Florida, Gainesville is home to the University of Florida's over 63,000 students, along with thousands of researchers, Gators fans, and university employees who give the city a unique college-town identity.

The city is surrounded by nature preserves, forests, and freshwater springs where locals can swim, kayak, and tube, while the downtown area has a growing restaurant, craft beer, and arts scene that keeps students busy year-round.

College football is especially important to local culture, with home games drawing dozens of thousands of fans to the school's Ben Hill Griffin Stadium throughout the fall.

The University of Virginia shapes Charlottesville's deep academic and historic identity, while the surrounding Blue Ridge foothills give the city easy access to some of Virginia's most scenic landscapes.

The university's campus sits near a lively corridor of restaurants and shops, while the pedestrian Downtown Mall serves as a center for dining, shopping, and live entertainment.

The surrounding region is also known for its unique wineries, farms, and natural mountain scenery.

School: Arizona State University

Arizona State University's sprawling Tempe campus gives the city a distinctly youthful energy within the larger Phoenix metropolitan area.

Historic Mill Avenue, directly beside campus, is lined with restaurants, bars, shops, and entertainment venues, becoming a major center of student activity at night.

The school's focus on research, technology, and entrepreneurship also bolsters Tempe's economy, while the city's location within the Phoenix metro area gives graduates access to one of the Southwest's largest job markets.

School: University of Michigan-Ann Arbor

Home to the University of Michigan and its over 50,000 students, Ann Arbor is the best and most distinct college town in the US.

College culture is deeply woven into the city's landscape, where campus buildings blend into a walkable downtown filled with restaurants, bookstores, cafés, bars, and cultural institutions.

Few traditions dominate the city like Michigan football, which attracts over 100,000 fans to Michigan Stadium during fall Saturdays, while maize-and-blue crowds fill the surrounding streets and businesses.

The unique combination of college sports, a lively downtown, a major research university, and a strong cultural scene makes Ann Arbor one of the country's quintessential college towns and ranks it at the top of this list.
