title: Can Oklahoma Make The College Football Playoff With A 9-3 Record? Paul Finebaum Thinks So...
description: The ESPN host claims the Sooners' brutal SEC gauntlet offers a rare lifeline, potentially rewarding a three-loss campaign with an unprecedented invitation to the expanded postseason
fullText:
Paul Finebaum isn't usually one to hand out easy paths, but he recently put Oklahoma in a small group of teams that could still reach the College Football Playoff even with three losses.

Speaking on The Paul Finebaum Show on ESPN Radio and the SEC Network, he laid it out clearly. "There are a couple of teams that would have a really good shot at making it at 9-3," Finebaum said. "Texas would be one. Oklahoma would be another. To get in with three losses, you better have played a significant schedule and nonconference. I think those are the two. LSU, probably because of playing Clemson."

Finebaum is acknowledging both the strength of Oklahoma's schedule and the reality of how the expanded playoff works. A tough slate can create a path that softer schedules simply don't have.

Still, history shows how difficult that path actually is.

No 9-3 team has ever made the College Football Playoff.

Two teams have gotten in at 10-3 — Clemson in 2024 and Alabama in 2025 — but both played in their conference championship games. That extra data point matters. A 9-3 team only plays 12 games and doesn't get the benefit of a 13th against another strong opponent in a title game.

Recent near-misses drive the point home. In 2024, Alabama sat at 9-3 and was the first team left out when 11-2 SMU got in. In 2025, Texas finished 9-3 and was the third team on the outside looking in. Those examples show that while the door isn't completely closed, it's a very narrow one.

The current playoff format makes it even tougher, with the new rules in place this season. Now, all four Power conference champions receive automatic bids, and Notre Dame gets an automatic berth if it finishes in the top 12 of the final CFP rankings. That setup locks in several spots and leaves fewer at-large opportunities for three-loss teams, no matter how impressive their résumés look on paper.

Finebaum isn't wrong that Oklahoma's schedule gives it a better shot than most. Games against Michigan, Georgia, Texas and the rest of a brutal SEC gauntlet create the kind of résumé strength the committee has historically rewarded. A couple of those wins, especially on the road or against ranked teams, would carry significant weight. But relying on a 9-3 finish still feels like playing with fire.

The more realistic and healthier goal for this team is 10-2 or better. A 10-2 record with Oklahoma's schedule would essentially lock up a playoff spot. That should be the standard.

The pieces are there for it — a healthy John Mateer, a loaded defense, and more experience across the roster than Brent Venables has had in previous seasons. The early stretch with Michigan, Georgia and Texas will go a long way toward deciding whether that 10-win threshold is reachable.

Finebaum's comment is fair in the sense that the door isn't completely shut at 9-3 for a team with this kind of schedule.

It's just a door that almost never opens.

Oklahoma is better off treating three losses as a worst-case scenario rather than a viable backup plan. Win the games they're supposed to win, take care of business in the middle of the league slate, and put themselves in position where the committee doesn't have to debate them.

The Sooners have already shown they can compete at a high level in the SEC. Last year's playoff appearance proved that. The next step is consistency and finishing with a record that removes any doubt.

Finebaum giving them a path at 9-3 is interesting. Making sure they don't need that path is the better approach.

title: How is former Auburn QB Ashton Daniels faring at FSU preseason camp?
description: The former Auburn starter is hoping to end his college career on a positive note at Florida State.
fullText:
Former Auburn quarterback Ashton Daniels produced solid numbers over the final portion of Auburn football's 2025 season. However, the Tigers' quarterback room was gutted with the hire of Alex Golesh, and Daniels was left needing to find a new home for his final season of eligibility.

He found that new home through the transfer portal in Tallahassee, Florida, and is poised to take over the starting quarterback role for Florida State in 2026. Florida State, like Auburn, is hungry to return to success this season, and Daniels will be tasked with leading the Seminoles to bowl eligibility for the first time since 2023.

How is Daniels faring in his new uniform? Florida State head coach Mike Norvell shared with the media this week that Daniels has shown signs of blemish, but is impressed with the former Tiger so far as the Seminoles prepare for the 2026 season.

"But he's been outstanding when it comes to knowing where to go with the ball, his ownership of the things we're asking him to do," Norvell said. "I would say it would challenge as good as what I've seen. Just the way that he's gone about that."

Since missing the 2023 College Football Playoff, Florida State has won just seven games over the last two seasons, and is working to return to the postseason picture. Daniels will get the chance to lead the Seminoles' offense and will rely on talented pieces, including wide receiver Duce Robinson, to achieve that goal.

Daniels initially lost the starting job to Jackson Arnold last season at Auburn, but made the most of his season by passing for 797 yards and three scores over the final four games of the 2026 season. He completed 49 passes for 612 yards over his final two starts against SEC rivals Vanderbilt and Alabama, throwing just one interception.

Daniels has proven during his time at Auburn and Stanford to be a quality passer, and worked to limit turnovers last season on the Plains. He will look to use his development as a senior for the Florida State Seminoles and end his collegiate career on a positive note.

title: Washington Football K Named to Preseason Lou Groza Award Watch List
description: The Washington Huskies could have one of the best kickers in college football this coming fall.
fullText:
Washington Huskies kicker Tyler Robles found himself among 35 specialists named to the 2026 preseason Lou Groza Award watch list.

Awarded annually to the best kicker in college football since 1992, no Husky kicker has won the honor, but several have been recognized on the preseason list, including most recently Grady Gross in 2024. Robles, a transfer addition from Texas State ahead of the 2026 season, proved to be one of the best kickers in the country last season.

Following two seasons at USC in 2023-24, the Encinitas, California native converted 21-of-23 field goal attempts and 53-of-54 extra points, leading the Bobcats in scoring with 116 points—a TSU record for points in a season.

The Lou Groza Award, presented by the Orange Bowl Committee, is given annually to the nation's top collegiate place-kicker in the NCAA Football Bowl Subdivision (FBS). The recipient is determined by a voting panel that includes NCAA Division I football head coaches, sportswriters, sportscasters, conference representatives, professional kickers, and previous award winners.

🏈 The road to the Lou Groza Award starts now!

The 2026 Lou Groza Award Preseason Watch List has officially been unveiled, featuring the nation’s top kickers to watch this season. ⚡👟

And in honor of the award’s 35th anniversary, we’re celebrating with a special Watch List of… pic.twitter.com/HgsoK55rez

Robles didn't get much of an opportunity to show his potential in his first two seasons in college with the Trojans as the 5-foot-7 kicker made just two appearances, both of which came as a true freshman in 2023 making one extra point attempt against Nevada with three kickoffs in the Holiday Bowl against Louisville—all of which came in the second half in the Trojans' 42-28 victory over the Cardinal in San Diego.

"It's very different," the new UW kicker said in his first media appearance during spring camp when asked about the differences between San Marcos, Texas, and Seattle. "I had a great time there. I love Seattle, though. I was very familiar with the area before I came here, which made it easy to make the transition. I left Seattle during the break. Did a lot of hiking, stuff outside, went to the UFC event at Climate Pledge."

The numbers Robles put up in his lone season in the Sun Belt Conference would put the fourth-year kicker in the top five for a single season in made field goals and one of the top three most efficient kickers in UW history.

With two seasons of eligibility remaining, Robles could cement himself as one of the best kickers in school history.

title: Dan Hurley: College Basketball in 2026 Is 'Total Chaos'
description: With the men's basketball roster set, UConn will not turn to the transfer portal after a Colorado judge ruled players in the Class of 2022 may return to college for a fifth year.
fullText:
Dan Hurley isn't about to jump into the transferportal, now that the ruling of a Colorado judge has made six or seven dozen playerseligible to play – at least for now, unless another court overturns that decision – in the 2026-27 season.

He made that clear Friday in speaking with reportersafter a team scrimmage. He's got the 15 men he plans to do battle with in theupcoming season, a campaign loaded with one A-list competitor after anotheruntil the rigorous Big East season begins.

Simply, Hurley will not be pursuing any of the membersof the Class of 2022 who have been granted a fifth year of eligibility.

"Our team is on the floor," he saidwithout hesitation.

Dog Days 😤 pic.twitter.com/DTb16mSNBV

Fans already know some of them: Demary,Mullins, Ross, Ball, another Ross.

Then there are the freshmen: Landrew. County.

And the transfers: Hines,Khamenia, Machowski, Nash and Shaw, Amosoz, Giltay and Džafic.

This is the roster Hurley and his staff put togetherin the weeks after their lossin the championship game of the Men's NCAA Tournament. A team created after they said goodbyeto five seniors and to four players who decided to search for a different landingspot in the transfer portal.

Each new player seemingly was selected to fill arole – experienced players either envisioned by Hurley as a starter or anecessary depth piece, freshmen intended to develop into standout collegeplayers.

An old-school coach assembled his team in anold-school manner.

Hurley has been coaching long enough that he knowsthe way college sports used to be – before NIL, before agents, before sharedrevenue, before the transfer portal and the havoc all of that has brought.

On Friday, he passionately conveyed his feelingsabout teams that are continuing to tinker with their rosters in the wake oflast week's ruling in Colorado.

👀 https://t.co/TYQ1XBn2u4 pic.twitter.com/obvbNKKvUf

"The art of what we do has been cheapened alittle bit," he said in his Friday media availability, speaking about the coachingprofession. "You can put together better teams, teams that can compete andnot have to identify young talent, develop that talent."

"Now," Hurley continued, "you can screw up highschool recruiting, you can screw up portal recruiting and not have a very goodteam, and start plucking from a group of players in August and put together ateam."

The ramifications of that? A team assembled at the lastminute, denied the time over the summer to jell. Players who had beenworking hard to gain an advantage in the battle for a starting spot, for example, suddenly finding themselves with a new role.

"Now, let's unleash 80 players into the sport in thefirst week of August. We can't go on like this. And anyone that acts like it'sgreat, it's fine, it's good for college basketball, they've already taken thestance that this is what they've wanted, and now they're just defending theirposition. It's total chaos and it's not sustainable."

title: College analysts lists one key reason why Badgers will be Big Ten contenders this season
description: Amid all the turnover, there’s one mainstay for the Badgers keeping them as a contender.
fullText:
Over the past few years, the Wisconsin Badgers have found a way to be successful in the Big Ten, finishing in the Top 5 in each of the past three years despite constant turnover with the roster.

Wisconsin has also done so without a top-tier Big Ten budget, which is expected to continue this year, as resources continue to increase significantly across the country. That's what prompted the departures of starters John Blackwell and Aleksas Bieliauskas in the offseason, with the former heading to Duke on a deal that is reportedly expected to exceed $4 million this season.

With Blackwell departing, the Badgers retained big men Nolan Winter and Austin Rapp, while adding Owen Foxwell, Trey Autry, Eian Elmer, and Victory Onuetu to the roster from either overseas or the transfer portal. Without that clear 1-2 punch like Wisconsin had with Blackwell and Nick Boyd last year, this season's team feels more system-oriented with quality fits across the board.

Does Wisconsin still have what it takes to be a contender in the Big Ten? Brian Butch believes so, and it's because of one key reason: Greg Gard.

"Because it's what they do. It's Greg Gard," Butch said about the Badgers being a sleeper Big Ten contender. "Like, I mean, that's all I need to say is Greg Gard, and everyone said, 'okay, yeah, that makes sense.' Like, I think part of it is though is they've invested. They had to pick with John Blackwell. Do you invest the majority of your budget with John, or do you go get Nolan Winter, Austin Rapp, and then fill around those 2 guys? I'm going to take 2 versus 1. In this day and age, it's irresponsible to go pay a guy a boatload of money, take half your budget away, and now all of a sudden, you're sitting there, you know, we got to fill a roster. I think that's part of what they're at.

"You will understand the way Wisconsin wants to play. They put money into the front court last couple of years, and I think the tournament success hasn't been there because of this. And I think Greg's has addressed that defensively. They got guys that are better. You look at Victory [Onuetu] from Hofstra, the big he's going to be there to be able to block shots, get aggressive. We've talked about every Big Ten team has invested in bigs, it seems like, 'okay, that's the one.'"

That fact about bigs has been true. We've now seen teams prioritizing size in the frontcourt and the possession battle be extremely successful over the past few years. The Florida Gators are one of those teams. Illinois is another. Tennessee did quite well this year. Duke had/has good size. Michigan, this year's winners, had a very dominant frontcourt. The examples go on and on.

Now, adding size does cost money, so Wisconsin had to be diligent with how its resources were spent. But they were able to retain two key bigs from last year, while adding Victory Onuetu to the depth on the bench with Will Garlock. That four should keep the Badgers more competitive in the frontcourt.

But there's also the system fits, such as Owen Foxwell and Eian Elmer, who seem to have bought in to what Wisconsin wants to do on both sides of the court.

"You talked about Owen Foxwell. I think he's going to be elite and what he's able to do," Butch continued. "I think this Wisconsin team is going to be more of a system-type offense than rely on one guy to go and make a play. The last couple of years, that's what it's felt like, whether it's John Tonje, whether it's been Nick Boyd, John Blackwell. They've been more, okay, go break a guy down, go score. I think now there's more system.

"And when you have more system on the offensive side, It really changes the way that defenses have to guard you. They've got to guard all 5. We know Wisconsin wants to spread it and really shoot more 3s, and get to the rim. They've done that. They've added that in [Eian] Elmer from Miami of Ohio, what he's able to do. So I think in general, the pieces are all there."

Now, the pieces have to come together. While that did happen offensively, and in a big way last year, the Badgers weren't as connected defensively, despite having some quality individual defenders. To return back to that top tier that Wisconsin showed in 2024-25, the Badgers need to be a more complete team with a top-30 defense.

title: Mason Awe, Three Rivers grad, named Emrick/Mielcarek Male Athlete of the Year
description: Awe excited for opportunity at Kalamazoo College, voted Athlete of the Year
fullText:
THREE RIVERS — Mason Awe knows the overall workload when he arrives at the college level will be a lot.

But he's ready for it. In carrying a solid effort in his time at Three Rivers High School both on the playing field and in the classroom, Awe understands what it will take to be successful.

Now, as he put it, he just has to continue to bring the work ethic on a daily basis. A challenge? Sure. Is he scared? Not gonna happen.

Awe was chosen as the recipient of the 2026 Corky Emrick & Tom Mielcarek Male Athlete of the Year award. The honor, presented by Sturgis Journal Sports Editor Brandon Watson, is a yearly one for a local graduating senior who played multiple sports throughout their high school tenure in addition to being a solid student and a strong member of the community.

Each year, a panel is put together by Watson, and votes are cast for nominated senior student athletes.

"You know, I think I'll miss seeing my friends every day. Coming into school, you know who you are going to see on a daily basis and who will be at school to talk to," Awe said of moving on. "Going to college, everyone will probably be going their own way. They'll each have their own things going on."

Awe will continue his football playing career with Kalamazoo College later this fall. The academic draw was a big one for Awe to Kalamazoo. He has a nice scholarship in his pocket and plans to make the most of it.

The decision, he said, came down to playing football or baseball at the next level.

"It came down to I love playing football, I like playing baseball. So part of the reason I picked K was because I love football," he said. "I could have an opportunity to play baseball there as well, but we will see what happens. Dual sporting is a lot."

The location of the school, its proximity to his home in Three Rivers and facilities were also positive pulls for Kalamazoo and Awe.

"It felt like the right place," he said.

Facing adversity is nothing new for the Three Rivers grad. He missed his entire junior season on the football field with a significant knee injury. But he was determined to get back onto the field of play at all costs and eventually came back to play that junior season for the Wildcat baseball team.

It helped propel him into his senior year on the gridiron.

"I think coming off that injury, getting a chance to play baseball as a junior, it really kept my confidence up going into football that fall," Awe said. "I wasn't being tackled in baseball, but I did a lot of the running and cutting with my legs, so I felt good. It was full-send; I had to trust it."

Awe returned for his senior season and helped lead the Wildcats to the MHSAA football playoffs.

At Kalamazoo, he plans to study either business or economics. Kalamazoo offers a major and minor to its undergraduate students, so Awe will have an option there as well. It could be political science, it might not.

"We're just gonna have to see where it goes," he said.

Growing up, football was everything outside of family for Awe. It even included family as he played for father Jeff in the purple and black. Awe has been throwing a pigskin since he could walk, and with dad being a coach, he was continually around the older players and soaking it all in.

"Summer workouts, always being around the older guys, and I couldn't wait to be in that position, to play on the big field," Awe recalled about being a youngster around the program. "It grew on me a lot. I will miss it, the Friday nights. Walking out those doors, the atmosphere, the band. It's just different."

The Kalamazoo College playbook will certainly be bigger than what Awe is used to. He admitted seeing it already and trying to become acclimated as early as possible. There's a lot to it, obviously, and with him being a future quarterback for the Hornets, he will be expected to know it from cover to end.

"I'll learn it; I'm not worried about that," he said.

The Hornets will open the season at home against Kenyon College (Ohio) at 1 p.m. Sept. 5.

title: Key transfer quarterbacks for the 2026 college football season: Josh Hoover has huge shoes to fill at Indiana
description: Josh Hoover is tasked with replacing Fernando Mendoza after Mendoza's Heisman-winning season and Indiana's national title.
fullText:
There are once again a lot of familiar quarterbacks in new places ahead of the 2026 college football season. Here are the most notable quarterbacks who changed schools during the offseason.

Arnold was Auburn's primary quarterback in 2025, but threw for just six touchdowns across 215 passing attempts in 10 games and transferred after Hugh Freeze's departure. The former highly touted Oklahoma recruit now heads west to play for former Florida coach Dan Mullen and hopes that his third school in four seasons will facilitate a breakout season.

With James Madison coach Bob Chesney now at UCLA, Barnett left for a power conference school too after leading the Dukes to the College Football Playoff in 2025. In two seasons as JMU's starter, Barnett threw for over 5,400 yards and 49 TDs to just 13 interceptions. He also rushed for 589 yards and 15 TDs in 2025.

The three-year starter at Iowa State will play his final season of college football in the Big Ten after following coach Matt Campbell to State College. Becht's stats dropped in 2025 as Iowa State won three fewer games than it did in 2024, but he tossed 64 career TDs and threw for 9,274 yards over 42 games with the Cyclones.

Boley was Kentucky's main quarterback in 2025 as the Mark Stoops era came to an ignominious end. Boley threw for 15 TDs and 12 interceptions in 2025 and now heads to Tempe as the favorite to start for coach Kenny Dillingham.

Brown was one of the most productive quarterbacks in college football a season ago and went to Auburn after ex-USF coach Alex Golesh joined the Tigers. Brown completed 66% of his passes for 3,158 yards and 28 TDs in 2025 while also rushing for 1,008 yards and 14 TDs in just 12 games.

Chiles came to Michigan State in 2024 after Oregon State coach Jonathan Smith was hired by the Spartans. The last two seasons did not go how both Smith and Chiles envisioned. As Smith was fired, Chiles is now at Northwestern after throwing for 23 TDs and 14 interceptions in 21 games in East Lansing.

Can Colandrea replicate his best season in Lincoln? After two seasons at Virginia, Colandrea transferred to UNLV for the 2025 season and threw for nearly 3,500 yards and rushed for almost 650. He scored 33 total touchdowns too.

Craig was a two-year starter for the Crimson and threw 48 TDs across 2024 and 2025. A season ago, Craig was 208-of-338 passing for 2,869 yards and 25 TDs with seven interceptions as Harvard made the FCS playoffs.

The Seminoles' hopes of a bounce-back season rest largely on Daniels, who played in just four games at Auburn in 2025. In those games, he threw for 797 yards and rushed for 280 while scoring five total touchdowns. In three seasons at Stanford, Daniels threw for 21 TDs and rushed for nine, but also threw 20 interceptions.

Edwards spent just one season at Wisconsin and played in just two games. An early-season knee injury sidelined Edwards for the rest of 2025 after he transferred from Maryland. Edwards has played just one full season of college football; in 2024 he threw for 2,881 yards and threw for 15 TDs with nine interceptions. Can he succeed for Bill Belichick?

Eget spent five years at San Jose State before transferring at the end of the 2025 season. He was the best quarterback available in the transfer portal after Darian Mensah's controversial transfer to Miami. Eget threw for 30 TDs and over 5,500 yards combined in his two seasons as the Spartans' starter.

All Hoover is doing is joining the defending national champions after a transfer quarterback led the Hoosiers to an undefeated season on the way to the Heisman Trophy. No pressure there at all.

Hoover emerged as TCU's starter in 2023 and completed 65% of his passes with the Horned Frogs. He's thrown for over 9,600 yards in his career along with 71 TDs. He's not afraid to go downfield, either. Hoover has a career average of 8.1 yards an attempt

The seventh-year quarterback is now at a non-power conference school. After two seasons at LSU and two seasons at Texas A&M, Johnson transferred to North Carolina before the 2024 season. A devastating knee injury in the season opener led to a grueling rehabilitation, but Johnson returned to play in four games in what was a lost season for the Tar Heels in 2025.

Joseph nearly joined the 3,000-1,000 club in 2025. In 12 games, Joseph threw for 2,624 yards and 21 TDs while rushing 158 times for 1,007 yards and 13 scores. He's now tasked with revitalizing a Wisconsin offense that has scuffled and nearly cost coach Luke Fickell his job at the end of the 2025 season.

After spending three seasons as a backup with the Buckeyes, Kienholz should take over as the Cardinals' starter. The former highly touted recruit appeared in just 12 games and his lone start came in the Cotton Bowl at the end of the 2023 season. Across those dozen games, Kienholz threw for 250 yards on 36 pass attempts and rushed 17 times for 68 yards.

It became clear at the end of the 2025 season that Lagway needed a fresh start even with a coaching change in Gainesville. Lagway completed 63% of his passes but threw for just 2,264 yards across 12 games and also had 14 interceptions. He threw five picks in a 20-10 September loss to LSU, and then three more in a blowout loss to Kentucky. Can Baylor kickstart his career?

The former Sun Devils QB was Lane Kiffin's big acquisition of the offseason after the ex-Ole Miss coach came to Baton Rouge. Leavitt's breakout season came in 2024 as he helped lead ASU to the College Football Playoff. He played in just seven games in 2025 because of a foot injury. In 20 games at ASU, Leavitt completed just over 61% of his passes for 4,513 yards and 34 TDs to just nine interceptions.

Lopez didn't have to move very far from Chapel Hill. After two seasons at South Alabama — and a strong 2024 season — Lopez was a symptom of the UNC dysfunction in 2025. He threw for 1,747 yards and 10 TDs across 11 games and rushed for just 133 total yards after he had 463 with the Jaguars in 2024.

Fernando's younger brother is in line to start for the Yellow Jackets after attempting just 25 passes in two seasons with the Hoosiers. Mendoza appeared in nine games in 2025 and threw for five TDs on 24 pass attempts. He also rushed for 190 yards on 13 carries thanks to a few big garbage-time runs.

Can Miami's offense be even better with Mensah at QB? The former Tulane QB threw for 3,973 yards and 34 TDs on 500 pass attempts in 2025 and completed over two-thirds of his passes. There's a reason Miami pushed so hard to get Mensah to replace Carson Beck. With RB Mark Fletcher and WR Malachi Toney back for 2026, Miami is a playoff favorite once again.

title: Bryan Kohberger's choice of 'a house full of women' may hold the key to the Idaho murders' biggest mystery
description: The Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare" explores whether Bryan Kohberger's struggles with women fueled the deadly attack.
fullText:
Bryan Kohberger took the motive for the Idaho murders to his prison cell. One filmmaker believes the answer may lie in why he chose the house he attacked.

"The fact that [this] was the house that he chose. This was a house that had five women living in it. The night that the murders happened, Xana Kernodle's boyfriend, Ethan Chapin, was over, but really, this was a house full of women, and it seems quite clear that he targeted it," Skye Borgman, director of the Netflix docuseries "The Idaho Murders: College Nightmare," told Fox News Digital.

"He watched the house; he was around the house in the days, weeks and months leading up to the murders," Borgman said. "So, it seems pretty likely that he had a very low regard, if not hatred, for women."

Idaho Murders: New Book On Kohberger Reveals Previously Unseen Evidence, Claims Sheath Could Be Inadmissible

"It's all conjecture, but he seemed to struggle with his relationships with women," Borgman explained. "And we look at this incel movement and the question of whether or not he was an incel, and whether or not he didn't like women."

"It seems to me that there was a hatred of women there," Borgman added.

Kohberger, 31, is serving four consecutive life sentences without the possibility of parole after pleading guilty to the 2022 stabbing murders of University of Idaho students Kaylee Goncalves, Ethan Chapin, Xana Kernodle and Madison Mogen at an off-campus rental home in Moscow, Idaho.

Before his arrest, former classmate Lilly Karaban recalled him as someone with a "his way or the highway" attitude who seemed to exist "in his own world."

WATCH: KAYLEE GONCALVES' MOTHER NOT SURPRISED BY KOHBERGER'S CLAIMS OF INNOCENCE, HOPES HE IS SENTENCED TO DEATH

Interviews, court records and accounts featured in the documentary described a series of troubling interactions involving Kohberger.

According to the documentary, classmates described him as "not particularly well liked," saying he frequently spoke down to women, engaged in "mansplaining" and became argumentative or aggressive during interactions. Several students said they found him "creepy" and that he made them feel uncomfortable.

"There were just strange incidents and strange behavior," Moscow Police Chief Anthony Dahlinger said in the documentary.

Former Washington State University Police Chief Gary Jenkins recalled another student's account of feeling cornered by Kohberger during an aggressive encounter. She also believed he occasionally followed her to her car. Kohberger was ultimately terminated from his teaching assistant position.

Jenkins said none of the reported incidents were referred to police because "nothing that occurred rose to the level of a crime."

Ed Jacobson, an FBI special agent involved in the investigation, said in the documentary that "we never saw evidence that shows Bryan Kohberger is part of the incel movement," an online community of mostly men who say they can't find romantic or sexual partners and often direct their frustration toward women.

"But Bryan Kohberger was very good at hiding his online activity," he noted.

For Borgman, the biggest question surrounding the Idaho murders remains the one Kohberger has never answered: why?

"I would love to, I think, along with the rest of the world, know why he did what he did," she told Fox News Digital. "But it is one of those things that I don't think any of us will ever know. That's a frustrating thing for myself ... and I know especially for the families. They wish so truly that he had been forced through the terms of his plea deal to give us more information about the why of it all."

In the documentary, Karaban said she believed Kohberger "has a thing against women based on the description of what he did to those poor three girls."

"People who brutalize women the way Kohberger did dislike them, find them threatening," she said. "So they take all that anger out on them."

Award-winning author James Patterson, who wrote a book on the case, previously told Fox News Digital his reporting uncovered multiple accounts of Kohberger engaging in unwanted interactions with women before his arrest.

At Seven Sirens Brewing Company in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, Kohberger would push his way into unwanted conversations with female bartenders and patrons. He went as far as asking for their addresses. Some women, according to the book, complained to the brewery's owner about "the creepy guy with the bulging eyes."

"Pretty much everybody we talked to just said, 'This is a strange man with a strange look — couldn't look people in the eye,'" Patterson said. "If he did look you in the eye, sometimes people wished that he hadn't. And his impression of himself was totally out of whack with the way other people perceived him."

In a police report obtained by Fox News Digital, an exotic dancer said a man she now believes was Kohberger visited the club where she worked in 2019, about two hours from his family's Pennsylvania home. She told investigators that while she was performing, the man remarked that he wanted to kill people. When she jokingly asked who, she said he replied, "Whoever I want."

Believing he was trying to get her attention, she alerted bouncers to keep an eye on him. She said the encounter didn't stand out again until she saw Kohberger's photo on television after his arrest and became fairly certain he was the man she had encountered.

Borgman believes Kohberger was trying "to commit the perfect crime."

"He failed in doing that," she said. "But I think his silence is a way of attempting to keep the spotlight focused on him."

Borgman said police are also "grappling with the why."

"We spoke to one of the FBI agents who worked the case, and he essentially says, 'You've got to be OK with not knowing,'" Borgman said. "And that's really hard for humans to do: be OK with not knowing. And to crawl inside somebody's mind and figure out the whys ... it's impossible. And I think that's one of the reasons people followed this case for so long. ... That question of the why still lingers with just about everybody."

After years of searching for answers, the victims' families are no longer waiting for them, Borgman said. Instead, they're focused on honoring their loved ones' legacies.

"I don't think they expect the perpetrator to talk," she said. " ... The families now are looking forward, not backward. ... Every one of them is committed to trying to help families who may be going through something like this."

"So while I don't want to say they're hopeful, every one of them is taking this tragedy and trying to make something good out of it because that's the only thing they can do," she said. "They can't carry around the hatred in their lives, or else it'll just consume them. So they carry the love forward. And the love is really with Ethan, Maddie, Kaylee and Xana."

Just two days before the documentary premiered on July 29, Kohberger made a dramatic bid to withdraw his guilty plea. He asked a judge to let him stand trial instead, alleging his attorneys pressured him into accepting a plea deal by promising better prison conditions and warning him about life on death row.

In his request, Kohberger said his attorneys didn't adequately represent him and that his guilty plea wasn't knowingly or voluntarily entered because it "was induced by unkept promises" and threats, The Associated Press reported.

In 2025, Kohberger said he was pleading guilty "freely and voluntarily." In doing so, he agreed to waive his rights to appeal, confirm that he understood the penalties for the crimes and assure the court that he wasn't coerced by his attorneys or anyone else to enter the plea. In exchange, prosecutors agreed not to seek the death penalty.

Borgman said some investigators involved with the case were so shaken by the crime and its impact on Moscow that "they don't work in law enforcement anymore."

"It's something that was too much, and they ended up leaving the police force," she said. "So it's important, I think, to really factor into what happened, the incredible toll it takes on law enforcement and the incredible toll it takes on the community."

"So many people felt fear," she said. "The fear was so deep that they weren't leaving their homes. And that fear, along with the arrest of the perpetrator, also led to this amazing feeling of community. It brought people together."

title: ESPN hypes SEC strength of schedule in latest myth-making exercise
description: The SEC is no longer the dominant conference in college football. Not only has the Big Ten won the last three national championships, but the SEC has also been soundly beaten in postseason games. But that’s not stopping the league from puffing out its chest once again. And it just so happens that their billion-dollar…
fullText:
The SEC is no longer the dominant conference in college football. Not only has the Big Ten won the last three national championships, but the SEC has also been soundly beaten in postseason games. But that’s not stopping the league from puffing out its chest once again.

And it just so happens that their billion-dollar rights partners at ESPN are helping push the narrative yet again.

It’s a cycle that seems to recur every year and makes college football fans feel as if they’re living their own version of Bill Murray’s Groundhog Day.

It’s a cycle that repeats itself continuously. SEC teams often have artificially inflated preseason rankings. Teams that have good early starts are rewarded with astronomical gains. The teams that lose aren’t punished because of the perceived strength of the opposition. Even though the SEC has been called out, the conference’s adherents (including plenty of voices on ESPN) treat it as definitive proof of superiority, even though it’s based more on conjecture and hypothetical wins than on what happens in reality.

And now the cycle is beginning all over again.

On Tuesday, the ESPN Insights page on X posted a list of teams ranked by the top strength of schedule coming into the 2026 college football season. The post touted the SEC expanding to a nine-game conference schedule and that, according to their metrics, every SEC team made the Top 20 of the rankings. Four Big Ten teams made the cut and none from any other conference.

This season, the SEC will start a 9-game conference schedule

A likely result of the additional conference game is that every SEC team has a strength of schedule in the Top-20, according to ESPN Analytics. pic.twitter.com/F5o3b9qomt

— ESPN Insights (@ESPNInsights) July 28, 2026

Immediately, social media was filled with comments and complaints that not only accused the network of stumping once again for their rights partner, but also the idea of devising strength-of-schedule metrics before a game has even been played.

“Because they play a bunch of SEC teams.”

“Really good, because they play a bunch of SEC teams.”

“How do you know if SEC teams are better than teams from other conferences?”

“They are better, because… https://t.co/cVUDLJ2Exo

— CougarStats (@CougarStats) July 28, 2026

ESPN owns the SEC Network.
 ESPN owns the Playoff broadcast.
 ESPN also builds the strength-of-schedule model that decides which SEC teams belong in the Playoff.
 That’s not a ranking. That’s manipulation. https://t.co/4aXU1Rrbnv

— Miles Shoaf || MSR (@milesashoaf) July 28, 2026

Rhett Lashlee at ACC media days last week:

“Whenever some of y’all figure out how we can have preseason strength of schedules and power rankings before anybody has played a game, y’all let me know.” https://t.co/ZfF3Uw1SQ2

— Steve Helwick (@s_helwick) July 28, 2026

You see, the SEC is tough because they play the SEC who plays the SEC which is tough because they play the SEC who is tough because they play the SEC who plays the SEC https://t.co/52ZI5NmV1E

— Shaloobys (@shaloobys) July 29, 2026

We’ve finally fully realized the SEC Strength of Schedule feedback loop https://t.co/qV0w4KShsX

— CF After Dark (@AfterDarkCF) July 28, 2026

ESPN wants you to believe that a conference that went 1-8 in the postseason vs P4 opponents, is much tougher now that they have the same amount of conf games as everyone else. https://t.co/HgSS88N1YI

— B1Gadier General Daniel A. Lanning (@DuckDMB) July 29, 2026

Allegations that ESPN improperly favors the SEC will always follow the company as long as subjective factors like this influence who has an opportunity to play for a national championship. We are supposed to believe that Ole Miss has one of the Top 5 hardest schedules in the country when they play teams like Auburn, Mississippi State, Missouri, and Florida? When their non-conference lineup features Wofford and Charlotte? Where they miss out on Alabama, Tennessee, and Texas A&M? While it may work with whatever analytics ESPN has produced, it doesn’t pass the common sense test.

The sensible thing to do would be to abolish preseason rankings and only start the process when the College Football Playoff committee releases its own rankings. Give us time to see who is actually good and who is not, and use what happens on the field to evaluate teams instead of projections and opinions. But expecting anything sensible to happen in the college football world means it’s not likely to occur anytime soon.

He set a single-season scoring record with 903 points that year and led the school to 93-11 record in his three seasons with three NCAA Tournament appearances before being selected No. 2 in the NBA draft.

PROGRAM RANKINGS: Top 25 | Big Ten | SEC | ACC | Big 12

Inducted into the Nevada hall of fame in 2025, Snyder led the Wolf Pack to the Western Athletic Conference regular season and tournament titles and the school's first Sweet 15 appearance as a senior in 2004. He was named WAC player of the year that season and scored 1,404 career points during his Reno days before being selected in the first round of the NBA draft.

The floor general for those UNLV Final Four squads also has a place in the school’s hall of fame. He handed out 838 assists and snared 275 steals over his four seasons with the Rebels. Anthony was a three-time, all-Big West selection and a third-team All-American in his senior season.

A standout infielder with the Rebels, Williams compiled 58 home runs and 217 RBI during his three seasons at the school. His best campaign was his final year when he hit 25 long balls and drove in 89 runs while being a first-team All-American selection. Williams was the No. 3 overall pick in the 1986 MLB draft and would go on to a 17-year career with 378 home runs.

Moore had one of the great seasons in men's collegiate golf in 2004 as he won the NCAA individual championship in addition to taking the U.S. Amateur title and victories in the the U.S. Amateur Public Links and the Western Amateur. The following year as a senior, Moore won the Haskins and Nicklaus Award with a scoring average of 69.29, the second-lowest in NCAA history.

UNLV’s all-time scoring leader in women’s basketball, Frohlich averaged 21.2 points and 10.1 rebounds with the Rebels from 1998-2002. She was a three-time Western Athletic Conference player of the year and third-team All-American as a senior. Frohlich competed for her native Germany on the national team and now operates a sports academy in California.

Kaepernick’s running mate in the Wolf Pack backfield was arguably just as instrumental to the team’s success during its epic 13-1 season in 2010. A third-team All-American as a senior, e recorded 5,159 yards from scrimmage, 4,588 of those rushing, and scored 53 total touchdowns for his Nevada career.

title: USA250: The 10 greatest college athletes from Nebraska
description: As part of USA TODAY Sports' USA 250 initiative, here's a look at the top 10 greatest college athletes to ever play in the state of Nebraska:
fullText:
Nebraska is a fascinating state to delve into in regard to college sports history, as it has a burgeoning sports scene without the imposing influence of professional sports.

The University of Nebraska's Memorial Stadium has sold out since the 1960s. The College World Series takes place in Omaha. Nebraska women's volleyball holds the world record for attendance at a women's sporting event.

And it isn't just a matter of circumstance. The programs built the loyalty. The Tom Osborne Nebraska-Oklahoma-Barry Switzer football rivalry is the stuff of legend, the 1990s Cornhuskers are still spoken of in reverential tones. Creighton basketball went from Missouri Valley powerhouse to Big East staple. And Nebraska women's volleyball has one of the most passionate followings among college sports as a whole.

From all of that loyalty is borne legendary figures. Across the state and across sports, Nebraska has the athletes to run with nearly any state in the country. Paring that list down to 10 proved to be an extremely difficult task. But here are the 10 Nebraska college athletes who managed to set themselves apart.

Nebraska of the 1990s was dominant. And Tommie Frazier was one of the team's great players in the decade. After he got his feet wet as a freshman, Frazier came into his own as a sophomore. Though he rarely threw the ball in Tom Osborne's ruthless triple option offense, but he passed for 3,521 yards in his career and added 1,955 yards and 36 touchdowns on the ground. But Frazier's legacy defies stats: Nebraska won 36 of 37 games in his final three seasons. The lone loss came to Florida State at the end of the 1993 season in the Orange Bowl that was a matchup of two unbeatens. Frazier would then lead the Cornhuskers to back-to-back titles the next two season and finish runner-up to Eddie George in the voting for the 1995 Heisman Trophy.

USA 250 LISTS: Alaska | Alabama | Arizona | Arkansas | California | Colorado | Connecticut | Delaware | Florida | Georgia | Hawaii | Idaho | Illinois | Indiana | Iowa | Kansas | Kentucky | Louisiana | Maine | Maryland | Massachusetts | Michigan | Minnesota | Mississippi | Missouri | Montana | Nebraska | Nevada | New Hampshire | New Jersey

Born in Omaha in 1935, Bob Gibson is one of the most dynamic pitchers in baseball history. His stuff is the stuff of legends, and he got his start with the Creighton Bluejays. A two-sport athlete, Gibson played baseball and basketball for his hometown university. He finished his career on the hardwood as the school's third-leading scorer at the time with 1,272 points. Unfortunately, his baseball stats are lost in the annals of history, it's known he was an outfielder and a pitcher for Creighton. Gibson had a legendary pitching career with the St. Louis Cardinals, and was named to Creighton's Hall of Fame in 1968.

When you think about hard-nosed Huskers, you think about Mike Rozier. After setting the single-season school record with 1,689 rushing yards as a junior in 1982, he shattered his own mark the following season as part of one of the greatest offenses in college history. Rozier put up an absurd 2,148 yards and an NCAA-record 29 touchdowns on the ground on his way to winning the 1983 Heisman Trophy. That Nebraska offense averaged over 50 points per game with Rozier serving as the focal point, and though it came up short of a national title with an Orange Bowl loss to Miami, it's remembered as one of the great seasons in Nebraska football.

PROGRAM RANKINGS: Top 25 | Big Ten | SEC | ACC | Big 12

Ask someone born in the '90s the most dominant defensive player they watched in college growing up, and dollars to donuts Ndamukong Suh's name is going to come up. One of the most overpowering linemen in history, Suh turned otherwise-stalwart offensive linemen into sleds. Suh's 2009 season is the stuff of college football legend: He finished fourth in Heisman Trophy voting, the best at the time for a solely defensive player since Steve Emtman in 1991 after logging 85 tackles with 20½ tackles for a loss and 12 sacks. Suh missing out on the Heisman was widely regarded as a death knell for the hopes of a solely defensive player winning the trophy, and he remains a Nebraska legend to this day.

Johnny Rodgers isn't just etched into the fabric of Nebraska. He's woven into the tapestry of college football. A receiver, running back, and return specialist, record after record fell before Rodgers' speed. A Walter Camp Player of the Year and Heisman Trophy winner in 1971, Rodgers finished his career with the two highest all-purpose yards seasons in Nebraska history, along with the record for most career all-purpose yards. He still holds the record for career receiving touchdowns and ended his time on the gridiron with the most points accounted for in Nebraska history. Often considered among the best return men in college football history, Rodgers was precursor for the athlete position in college sports.

Eric Crouch evokes one of the last gasps of an era of greatness for Nebraska football. Crouch led the Big 12 in rushing touchdowns in each of his final three seasons and posted a 35-7 record as a starter. He had a dominant senior campaign in 2001 to win the Heisman Trophy, edging out Florida quarterback Rex Grossman. For the season, Crouch rushed for 1,115 yards and 18 touchdowns and threw for 1,510 yards, while leading the Cornhuskers to the Bowl Championship Series title game in the Rose Bowl. Though Nebraska would lose to Miami (Fla.) in his final game, Crouch's legacy has endured as one of the most dynamic athletes in Cornhusker football history.

While Nebraska football is a dynasty, Nebraska volleyball is an institution all of its own. The Cornhuskers are five-time national champions and have four championships since the turn of the century. Pavan is one of the most decorated volleyball players in Nebraska history. She was a four-time first-team All-American and set multiple records with the Cornhuskers while making Lincoln a destination for volleyball. Pavan helped Nebraska to a national championship in 2006 and four consecutive Big 12 titles. She is quintessentially Nebraska volleyball, and volleyball is quintessentially Nebraska.

Why wouldn't Nebraska get two volleyball players on this list? Joining Pavan is Jordan Larson, who was also part of the 2006 championship team. Larson was a three-time All-American and had over 1,000 kills and digs in her Nebraska career. Her best season was in 2008, when she earned multiple accolades before becoming an Olympic star as well, culminating in a gold medal win in Tokyo in the 2020 Summer Games.

Fresh off her college career when she was a four-time first-team All-American, Frahm is already a Nebraska softball legend. Born in Papillion, Frahm started her career at Oklahoma, winning two national championships with a 44-2 record as the star pitcher for Sooners. Frahm transferred to Nebraska after her sophomore season, but was injured in her first game in 2024. She returned the following year to help Nebraska to the super regionals for the first time since 2014. Frahm was national player of the year as a senior, leading the Cornhuskers to their first Women's College World Series appearance since 2013,. A true two-way superstar, she posted a 47-14 record pitching over two seasons at Nebraska with an ERA of 1.44. She slugged 1.418 as a Cornhusker with 43 home runs.

title: USA250: The 10 greatest New Jersey college athletes ranked
description: Princeton and Rutgers are the two biggest university represented on our list of the 10 greatest college athletes from the state of New Jersey.
fullText:
From Ellis Island to the Jersey Shore to Asbury Park and the Stone Pony, the very town where Bruce Springsteen first lit up the stage, New Jersey is home to many things.

It’s also home to a deep roster of NCAA programs, including eight Division I universities, an Ivy League lacrosse powerhouse in Princeton and the "Birthplace of College Football" at Rutgers in New Brunswick. Two of its mid‑majors, St. Peter’s and Fairleigh Dickinson, have etched their names into March lore as unforgettable tournament Cinderellas.

And that’s only the surface of the state’s athletic legacy. Some of the nation’s top professional stars first built their careers at colleges across The Garden State.

So, here is the 100%, completely definitive (and surely unanimous) top 10 athletes to compete in college sports in New Jersey:

Bradley is considered one of the greatest athletes in Princeton athletics history and one of the most prolific men's basketball players of his time. A three-time All-American, Bradley is the program’s all-time points leader with 2,503 career points scored, a record he set without making a single 3-point shot and in just three years with freshmen ineligible to play. He’d also captain the United States Olympic men’s basketball team at the 1964 Tokyo Summer Olympics, where they won gold, while still in college. Highlights of his career include leading Princeton to its only Final Four in 1965 when he scored 58 points against Wichita State in the third-place game, which remains the second-highest total in tournament history. After completing his player career, he was a Rhodes Scholar, member of two New York Knicks championship teams and a U.S. Senator for the state of New Jersey.

Lloyd wasted no time becoming one of the best collegiate women’s soccer players in the country during her time at Rutgers, a path that led her to becoming one of the most decorated United States women's national team players.  The New Jersey product led the Scarlet Knights to the Sweet 16 as a freshman in what was the program's second-ever tournament bid. while setting program's single-season points record as a freshman at 37, with 15 goals and seven assists leading the way. A two-time All-American and the 2004 Big East midfielder of the year, Lloyd finished her career as the program’s all-time points (117) and goals scored (50) leader. Both records remain today. She is also tied for third with 15 game-winning goals scored.

USA 250 LISTS: Alaska | Alabama | Arizona | Arkansas | California | Colorado | Connecticut | Delaware | Florida | Georgia | Hawaii | Idaho | Illinois | Indiana | Iowa | Kansas | Kentucky | Louisiana | Maine | Maryland | Massachusetts | Michigan | Minnesota | Mississippi | Missouri | Montana | Nebraska | Nevada | New Hampshire | New Jersey

Dick Kazmaier is not Princeton’s only Heisman Trophy winner but is the last player from the Ivy League to receive college football's highest individual honor. Known to be a weapon in the Tigers’ single-wing offense, Kazmaier, who played halfback, kicker and quarterback, finished his career as Princeton’s all-time rushing leader (1,950 yards) and ranked second in passing (2,404 yards). In his Heisman Trophy season in 1951, Kazmaier led the Tigers to a perfect 9-0 season and No. 6 national ranking while rushing for 861 yards and nine touchdowns and throwing for 966 yards and 13 touchdowns.

Rice is not only one of Rutgers' greatest running backs, but one of the top players the program has ever produced. Coming off a standout freshman season with just over 1,110 rushing yards, Rice exploded for 1,754 yards and 20 touchdowns on 335 carries the next season. That’d earn him a seventh-place finish in the Heisman Trophy race. He led the nation the following season with 2,012 rushing yards and 25 touchdowns, earning first-team All-America honors and being selected as a Doak Walker Award finalist. He finished his Rutgers career with three consecutive 1,000‑yard seasons — a first in program history — and totaled 4,926 rushing yards and 50 touchdowns (49 rushing).

If Bradley was the greatest to step on the court for Princeton, then Sellers certainly was that for Rutgers. While Dick Vitale was an assistant and head coach at the school, he averaged 21.0 points and 9.8 rebounds in four seasons with the Scarlet Knights. He led Rutgers to its first ever NCAA Tournament and Final Four appearance his junior and senior seasons, respectively. Sellers averaged 19.2 points and 10.2 rebounds per game and was a second-team All-American in his senior season in 1976, the same year the Scarlet Knights finished with a 31-2 record after winning their first 31 games. Sellers would complete his career as Rutgers' all-time scoring and rebounding leader with 2,399 points and 1,115 rebounds. He was also a third-team All-American in 1975.

PROGRAM RANKINGS: Top 25 | Big Ten | SEC | ACC | Big 12

One of the more recognizable United States men’s national team players from the 1990s, Lalas serves the same recognition amongst former Rutgers athletes. A third-team All-American as a sophomore and junior, he won the Hermann Award — soccer’s version of the Heisman Trophy — during his senior season as he helped Rutgers to a 15-match unbeaten streak and the program's first No. 1 ranking. He led Rutgers to a combined record of 71-15-8 in his four seasons "On The Banks." He also led the program to three NCAA tournaments, which included appearances in the national semifinal in 1989 and the national championship game in 1990.

Known primarily as a second baseman in his Hall-of-Fame Major League career, Biggio spent three seasons as Seton Hall’s catcher and helped the program to a 121-55 overall record and a Big East title in 1987. A two‑time All-Big East first‑team selection and All‑American as a senior, Biggio hit .342 for his career and still holds the program record for triples (18). He also ranks second in runs scored (194) and is tied for fifth in home runs (27).

Hubbard is one of the greatest to ever put on the Princeton lacrosse jersey and one of the best goal scorers in college lacrosse history. A three‑time All‑American, Hubbard delivered one of the program’s defining moments in its rise to a national powerhouse with his overtime game‑winner in the 1996 NCAA title against Virginia, giving Princeton its first national title. He’d then help lead the Tigers to the next two Ivy League and national championships, strengthening their rise and dominance in the sport under Bill Tierney. Hubbard finished his career as Princeton’s all-time leading goals scorer with 163 goals and is now second all‑time in career goals and sixth in points (211).

Todd Frazier was a productive bat for the Scarlet Knights from the moment he arrived on campus, Frazier drove in 36 runs and hit nine home runs as a freshman. His best season came as a junior in 2007 when he blasted a program single-season record 22 home runs, drove in 65 runs, while leading Rutgers to a Big East tournament title and an NCAA berth. He went 13-for-25 at the plate with 12 runs scored, five walks and three home runs in six games at the Big East tournament that season. Just the third Rutgers player taken in the first round of the MLB draft, he ranks second in career home runs (42) and first in runs scored (210).

A multi-sport athlete, Pearce, who later changed her surname to Rampone, showcased her versatility at Monmouth, where she played soccer, basketball and lacrosse. It was on the soccer pitch where she quickly became her signature. Pearce dominated the Northeast Conference, a four-year career with the Hawks that helped her eventually make the U.S. women’s national team and, ultimately, win four Olympic medals. A two‑time Northeast Conference player of the year winner, she still owns the school career records for goals (79), assists (54), and points (212).

title: Who has the best college football stadium? Our top 25 rankings starts with LSU
description: Across the country, there are notable college football stadium that welcome fans on weekends in the fall. What are the best ones? Here's our list of 25:
fullText:
Few topics in college sports will divide respective fans than discussion the merits of their football stadiums. Saturdays in the fall are full of things that supporters hold dear. The traditions of game day, the pageantry and the success of their teams are something to be treasured by students and alums.

But we still accepted the challenge of trying to identify the 25 best stadiums with 10 staffers from USA TODAY Sports weighing in with their perspective using their own criteria. Some valued the visual element at top their list. Some considered the traditions or the difficulty of experience for opponents.

The final list includes locales from across the country in conferences big and small. The SEC dominates the representation with the Big Ten following behind in second. But there are plenty of are others included. Here’s the top 25 that is sure to inspire debate from readers:

A night game in Baton Rouge is an animal unlike any other. Bear Bryant described Tiger Stadium as “the worst place in the world for a visiting team.” LSU fans specialize in tailgating, full of culinary delights and plenty of imbibing. Then the game starts with the hostility on display that gives opposing players and fans something to forget. One thing to remember? The singalong for "Garth Brooks and "Callin' Baton Rouge."

The Horseshoe is one of the great venues in college football and one of the toughest places to win. The Buckeyes have lost just three games at home since 2016. Two of those losses have come in the rivalry against Michigan. Basically, any trip to Columbus with a crowd of more than 100,000 mostly against your team is as close to a guaranteed loss as you’ll find in the Power Four.

There are few better spectacles than Penn State's annual "White Out" games. It's especially intimidating in the evening when fans dress in white to provide visitors with an unsettling, eye-popping backdrop. Combined with the deafening roar provided by 100,000-plus fans, this makes Beaver Stadium one of the elite settings in the FBS.

Kyle Field supplies the SEC’s most singular experience. Yeah, there are some odd chants, routines and hand signs from the school's Aggie Yell Leaders. But the 12th Man is indefatigable, and the Aggies storming out of the tunnel to “POWER” before kickoff, while the stadium shakes, creates a scene suited for football heaven. A handful of SEC venues are tougher on road teams, but few stadiums are as memorable as this massive cathedral, especially when the fans sway in unison to the "Aggie War Hymn."

Size doesn't matter in the case of Autzen Stadium. While only boasting a capacity of 54,000, Oregon's home field is one of the classes of the Big Ten and toughest places to place. The Ducks have lost just twice at home since hiring Dan Lanning in 2022. This stretch rivals the most dominant run of play at home in program history, a 21-game winning streak under former Chip Kelly that ended with a loss to Southern California in 2011.

The environment "Between the Hedges" has made the Bulldogs nearly unbeatable at home under coach Kirby Smart. While the literally barking from Georgia fans doesn't always rattle your eardrums, Sanford Stadium can rumble when challenged. Georgia’s .918 home winning percentage during the Kirby Smart era is a credit to the program Smart built. It’s also a credit to Bulldogs fans.

STADIUM RANKINGS: Big Ten | SEC | ACC | Big 12

Simply put, Neyland Stadium is "a different type of loud," which is how former Oklahoma quarterback Baker Mayfield described playing there. And when the home team is thriving and “Rocky Top” plays on a loop, it’s pure psychological torture. Former Notre Dame quarterback Brady Quinn called it “the loudest place I ever played.” So loud, he said, the ball would tremble on the turf between plays.

There might be no other stadium that is a pictorial stand-in for college than the "The House that Rockne Built." Looming outside the stadium wall is the mural of "Touchdown Jesus" that overlooks the field. Lines and lines of some of the sport's most memorable coaches and players. National championships galore. While the vibe might be different than that seen at some of the larger SEC fields, no one can deny that Notre Dame Stadium occupies a special place in the sport's landscape.

You want history? How about the field where both Bear Bryant and Nick Saban walked the sideline while winning national championships by the bunches? It's also one of the toughest places to win. Alabama is 65-3 at Bryant-Denny the past 10 seasons. When 100,000 sets of crimson-and-white pompoms start shaking in the stands, you know: It’s over.

Florida fans singing Tom Petty's "I Won't Back Down" before the fourth quarter might be a new tradition. It's also peak college football. The Swamp can roar with the best of them, even if the Gators haven't matched their glory years in recent seasons. Consider last season: Florida went 4-2 at home, including an upset of Texas, and 0-6 away.

If you're looking for a stadium with a specific identity, Clemson Memorial Stadium has plenty to offer. There's one of the most raucous atmospheres in the ACC with more than 80,000 fans backing the home team. Between the Death Valley moniker, Howard's Rock, and the run down "The Hill," not to mention Clemson's historical success, it's hard to top the intimidation factor on college football Saturdays.

As great as the Big House is, size doesn't always matter the most. The largest venue in college sports is also the largest by seating capacity in the Western Hemisphere and the third largest in the world. At times, the Wolverines appreciated when the 100,000-plus crowd can influence the visitors, though bowl layout means the noise never quite seems to match the number of fans in the seats.

Nestled among the mountains in Provo, Utah, LaVell Edwards Stadium provides an intimidating presence for visiting teams with the crowd right on top of the field. There are not many panoramic views better in college football with one of the notable features being Y Mountain rising above the stands with a logo painted on its slopes that mirrors the one on BYU helmets. For those inclined to hike to the Y, you can do it with some effort. The path is short but very steep.

Husky Stadium might not register among college fans as one of the loudest stadiums in college football, however it absolutely stands with the elite when Washington is playing well. Fans watching on television can detect cameras shaking from the sound and raucous fans. But this ranking isn't just about sound. Husky Stadium also is one of the sport’s most beautiful backdrops and one of the coolest traditions: the “sailgating” boats checking out the action from Lake Washington.

Another place that has seen its home team have better days, Jordan-Hare still is regularly packed with Tigers fans who turn up the volume and influence the game. And how do you top a pregame ceremony with War Eagle flying around the stands? It's a truly unique environment, and nobody beats Auburn at swag surfing.

When talking about Lane Stadium, you begin with the start of the game. One of the great entrances in the sport takes place with Metallica's "Enter Sandman" blaring on the speakers and fans jumping up and down. The scenery surrounding Blacksburg provides spectacular fall colors that may not be appreciated on television. Should the Hokies return to the glory days of Frank Beamer, the fans will have played a significant part.

Not many places celebrate a touchdown better than Oklahoma with two Shetland ponies named Boomer and Sooner pulling a stagecoach across the field to celebrate. It's a portrait of Americana. The "Palace on the Prairie" lags a bit behind the stadiums with six-figure capacities, but it can still have its moments of urging on the home team to success and causing issues for the visitors.

Rice-Eccles Stadium is one of the few college football stadiums that have hosted an opening ceremony of the Olympics, but it mostly is one of the more difficult places for opponents to play. Helped by a student section dubbed the Mighty Utah Student Section, Utah boasts a 47-13 record at home since 2016, and the mark is more impressive at night with 29 wins in 35 games under the lights in the past 10 seasons.

The Badgers might have taken a step back in their success on the field, but the traditions at Camp Randall remain elite. None is more memorable than the “Jump Around” stampede at the end of the third quarter, which began in 1998 and was the soundtrack to the Badgers’ development into a powerhouse under former coach Barry Alvarez.

Occupying a picturesque location along the Hudson River, Michie Stadium sits in the middle of the United States Military Academy. There are not many better scenes in college football than the march-on with the Army cadets in formation prior to kickoff. You're experiencing patriotism and tradition rolled into one. The Black Knights might not be the best team on the field, but that's a bonus to an afternoon worth experiencing.

Sometimes it's something not part of the game that makes a stadium unique. One of the best scenes in college football comes at the end of the first quarter of Iowa home games. “The Hawkeye Wave” has players and fans turn to wave to the patients at Stead Family Children's Hospital overlooking the stadium. Kinnick is also a difficult place to play with the Hawkeyes compiling a 27-8 mark at home since 2021.

Admittedly, the Texas fans don't consistently produce a decibel level to match the capacity of more than 100,000. But for big games, the environment can be impressive. Texas is 13-1 at home since joining the SEC. As a certain Texas supporter who’s often found along the sideline would say: All right, all right, all right.

Let's be clear: The scene at the Rose Bowl is unlike any other when it hosts a game on New Year's Day. The scene for a Bruins home game lacks the same pageantry and tradition because the atmosphere is more muted with fewer fans in attendance and games not timed to have the sun set over the San Gabriel Mountains at the optimal time. But it's still worthy of inclusion for the shear history that drips from the time you make your way up to the stadium until you leave your seat at the end of the game.

Death. Taxes. A sellout for a Nebraska home game. Those are three things that have been certain since the start of the school's attendance streak in 1962. Despite the Cornhuskers being less significant on the field, this is one of the most iconic spots in college football. The fans provide one of the unique features of support when they release red and white balloons after the first Nebraska touchdown, though the tradition occurs less frequently.

Long one of college football’s most underrated venues, Williams-Brice is getting overdue respect the past few years. Never mind that South Carolina isn’t a blue blood or that they copied the hedges look of Georgia. When “Sandstorm” plays and those white towels wave, or when the crowd turns up the decibels on third down, you know you’re at a special place that packs a punch.

title: Texas Tech football officially enters Will Hammond era
description: The Texas Tech football program officially announced its new starting quarterback for the 2026 college football season on Friday. Will Hammond is the Red Raiders’ starting quarterback after the program announced the news via Texas Tech’s official X account. MORE:…
fullText:
The Texas Tech football program officially announced its new starting quarterback for the 2026 college football season on Friday.

Will Hammond is the Red Raiders’ starting quarterback after the program announced the news via Texas Tech’s official X account.

MORE: 8 top recruits to watch in college football for 2026

Hammond has been with the Red Raiders for the last two seasons, but has played sparingly. He finished the 2024 season with 471 yards through the air, two touchdowns and two interceptions. In 2025, he threw for 680 yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions.

Hammond takes over for Behren Morton, who started for the Red Raiders last season. Morton compiled 2,780 yards through the air, 22 touchdowns and six interceptions. Morton completed 66 percent of his passes.

The Red Raiders had a fantastic 2025 season, finishing 12-2. Texas Tech won the Big 12 and earned a bye in the College Football Playoff before falling to the Oregon Ducks in the quarterfinals. Hammond will try to take them back to the CFP this season.

The first game of the Hammond era will take place on Sept. 5 against the Abilene Christian Wildcats. The game will be at home for the Red Raiders before they head west to play the Oregon State Beavers on Sept. 12.

The Red Raiders will then come home to play the Houston Cougars on Sept. 18 in their Big 12 opener.

Kickoff for the game between the Red Raiders and Wildcats on Sept. 5 will be at 7 p.m. ET on FS1. All three of the Red Raiders’ first three games will be in prime time.

The four players on offense include quarterback Noah Fifita, offensive linemen Tristan Bounds and Alexander Doost, and wide receiver Tre Spivey. Fifita returns for one final season in Tucson after throwing for 3,228 yards and 29 touchdowns. He has also been named to the preseason all-Big 12 team and Allstate AFCA Good Works Team.

title: Jensen Huang made his $172 billion fortune on AI chips. His family’s $75 million gift to Vanderbilt argues art decides what technology is for
description: The $75 million gift to establish an art, architecture and design college is the largest Huang has ever made to a university.
fullText:
Jensen Huang has been on a bit of a philanthropic streak, having donated one of his iconic leather jackets to raise nearly $1 million for the Edge Institute, a nonprofit that brings together people working in tech, science, culture, and society to live together in pop-up villages and work on experiments.

What concerns exist about the CCA-Vanderbilt transition?

What happened to California College of the Arts?

Why did Nvidia's CEO donate to an art school?

How is Vanderbilt expanding its university presence nationally?

Now the Nvidia CEO and his wife, Lori, are making a somewhat unexpected turn, donating $75 million to Vanderbilt University for its art, architecture, and design San Francisco campus. It might seem odd for one of the world's most prominent technology leaders to donate to an art school, but the Huangs have interesting reasoning.

"Technology expands what we can build. Art and design determine why we build it," Huang said in a statement. "Together they shape civilization."

Pending approval, the gift will establish the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design, which is "envisioned as a hub" for creatives, according to Vanderbilt. The goal is to establish a school focused on advanced tech breakthroughs, art and architecture, developing technical and visual mastery through studio practice and design labs, and also to help students build both business and tech fluency. The gift has already spurred more than $25 million in additional donations, for a total investment topping $100 million so far.

With that context, it makes a little more sense why Huang, CEO of a $5 trillion AI chips company would be invested in the future of art and tech convergence. And it isn't his first move here. The San Francisco campus is taking over the site of the California College of the Arts, the 119-year-old institution that will graduate its final class in 2027 after struggling with falling enrollment and a roughly $20 million deficit. Huang had backed CCA before its collapse, according to the San Francisco Standard. His combined giving to CCA and Vanderbilt now approaches $97.5 million, according to the Standard, making the Vanderbilt gift his largest ever to a university, topping the more than $50 million he has given his alma mater, Oregon State.

San Francisco is also the logical home for the school, as opposed to Nashville, where its flagship university sits, because it puts students at the epicenter of new technology development.

"This college, together with additional academic programming under development, will prepare creative leaders to shape culture, industries and communities in San Francisco's thriving economy, nationally and around the world," Chancellor Daniel Diermeier said in a statement.

title: SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey says talk of leaving the NCAA is "real"
description: As college football tries to navigate an era of chaos sparked by the reckoning from decades of antitrust violations, one of the most powerful conference claims it's serious about leaving the NCAA.
fullText:
As college football tries to navigate an era of chaos sparked by the reckoning from decades of antitrust violations, one of the most powerful conference claims it's serious about leaving the NCAA.

Via Nick Schultz of On3.com, SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey said Monday that his conference could indeed break away and do its own thing.

“You phrased the question, ‘How real?’ So I’ll take that as, like, real or not. So they’re real,” Sankey said. “People have talked about that. They’ve opined about the frustrations that bring them to the point of saying we should look at something significantly different."

Sankey claims he's not simply trying to secure an edge for the SEC in ongoing discussions regarding the future of college football.

“I do not believe that is a leverage point — I think that’s just honest communication," Sankey said. "I would prefer that stay in a meeting room or on a video conference and not be part of the D1 ticker the next morning, but I don’t control all of that.”

Leverage or not (and no leverage is worth a damn if the party exercising admits it's leverage), something has to give. And if the proposed solution harms the biggest conferences, why should they go along with it?

While recent years have seen a revolution in college football, the next phase could be an evolution in which major conferences run their own leagues, perhaps with (in time) a postseason tournament consisting of the best teams in each conference.

With the NCAA losing much of its power, the conferences can fill the void. With so many college football teams, maybe the best solution is to have several different leagues that run their own businesses. The various conferences can then do their own thing. Once the conferences are sorted out, the postseason arrangements will follow.

title: How young is the average age of Texas football’s roster?
